meta.blurb: Mr Utterson hears about a small, pale man who tramples a child and walks on, and about a door nobody likes to discuss. The man is Hyde, and he has a strange hold on Utterson's old friend, Dr Jekyll.
meta.bible: Mr Gabriel Utterson: a London lawyer, plain, serious and loyal, the main point of view. Mr Richard Enfield: his cousin and Sunday walking companion, a lively man about town. Dr Henry Jekyll: a rich, kind and respected doctor, friend of Utterson; secretly the maker of the Potion. Mr Edward Hyde: a small, pale, hateful young man who seems deformed though no one can say how; the dark side of Jekyll. Dr Hastie Lanyon: a doctor and old friend of Jekyll, who quarrels with him and dies of shock. Poole: Jekyll's loyal butler. Sir Danvers Carew: a kind old Member of Parliament, murdered by Hyde. Mr Guest: Utterson's clerk who knows handwriting. Inspector Newcomen: the police officer from Scotland Yard. Soho: the poor district of London where Hyde lives. Cavendish Square: where Lanyon lives. Regent's Park: where Jekyll changes without the Potion. London: the city of fog and gaslight. Key objects: the Door in the back street, the Cheque, the Cane that Utterson gave Jekyll, the Cabinet and laboratory behind Jekyll's house, the Potion made from a powder or Salt, the Statement. Voice and tone: sombre, steady and suspenseful, a mystery told by Utterson that is solved only at the end by two letters; deaths are stated plainly with no gore; the transformation is chemical, never magic. The story follows Robert Louis Stevenson's Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886), which is in the public domain. Added places and names: Gerrard Street: Hyde's address in Soho. Messrs Maw: the chemists who sold Jekyll his salt. Bradshaw: Jekyll's footman. Denman: the surgeon who built the old dissecting theatre. Portland Street: where Hyde hides in a hotel. Coutts: the bank. The Square: where Jekyll's house stands. Chapters follow the novella's order: the Door, the Search, the Dinner, the Murder, the Cane, the Letter, the Peace, Lanyon's death, the Window, Last Night, Lanyon's Narrative and Jekyll's Statement.
chapters: My Life Is at Your Mercy
A New Face in the Glass

beats.scene: Mr Utterson, a plain-faced lawyer, walks through a foggy London street.
beats.summary: Mr Utterson, a lawyer of London, is introduced as a plain, lean and unsmiling man.

beats.scene: Utterson sits alone at his table with a plain glass of gin.
beats.summary: He drinks gin alone to curb his taste for fine wine, has not seen a play in twenty years, and still forgives other men's faults.

beats.scene: Utterson and Enfield walk side by side along a busy London pavement.
beats.summary: His closest friend is his distant cousin Enfield, and every Sunday the two walk together through London.

beats.scene: Two men turn into a narrow back street full of bright shops.
beats.summary: One Sunday their walk takes them down a by-street in a busy quarter of London, where the shops look prosperous.

beats.scene: A blistered door in a windowless wall, with no bell or knocker.
beats.summary: Two doors from a corner, a gloomy windowless block of building pushes into the street, with a shabby door that has no bell.

beats.scene: Enfield raises his walking stick and points at the shabby door.
beats.summary: Enfield stops, points his stick at the door, and asks whether Utterson has ever noticed it; it is linked in his mind with a very odd story.

beats.scene: A lamplit empty street at three in the morning in winter.
beats.summary: Enfield begins his tale: he was coming home at three o'clock on a black winter morning through streets of lamps and no people.

beats.scene: A small man hurries along one street while a girl runs down another.
beats.summary: Enfield sees a small man walking briskly east and a girl of about eight running down a cross street, and the two reach the corner together.

beats.scene: The small man walks over a fallen girl, who lies screaming on the ground.
beats.summary: The man runs into the child, knocks her down, and calmly tramples over her without a glance, leaving her screaming.

beats.scene: Enfield runs down the empty street after the small man.
beats.summary: Enfield shouts, runs after the man, seizes him by the collar and brings him back to the screaming child.

beats.scene: Angry neighbours and a doctor surround the small man in the lamplight.
beats.summary: The girl's family and a doctor arrive; the doctor turns white with anger at the man, who stands cold and sneering.

beats.scene: The small man shrugs coldly and names a price in the lamplight.
beats.summary: The man says that if they wish to make money from an accident he is helpless, and asks them to name a sum; they ask for a hundred pounds.

beats.scene: The small man unlocks the shabby door with a key and goes inside.
beats.summary: To fetch the money, the man leads them to this very door, unlocks it with a key, and returns with ten pounds in gold and a cheque for the rest.

beats.scene: Enfield, the doctor and the small man sit up together until the bank opens.
beats.summary: Enfield doubts the cheque, so he keeps the man with him, and the three of them wait at his chambers until the bank opens.

beats.scene: Enfield hands a cheque across a polished bank counter.
beats.summary: Enfield himself hands in the cheque at the bank, saying he thinks it a forgery; the clerk tells him it is perfectly genuine.

beats.scene: Enfield swings his cane and shakes his head as the two cousins walk.
beats.summary: Enfield calls it a bad story: a detestable man, a respected signer, and a likely blackmail, so he calls the house Black Mail House.

beats.scene: A court behind high buildings, with three closed windows and a smoking chimney.
beats.summary: Enfield never asks questions about the house, but he has studied it: there is no other door, three clean windows on the court and a chimney that smokes.

beats.scene: Utterson walks on with his head down, thinking hard.
beats.summary: Utterson praises Enfield's rule and then asks the name of the man who trampled the child; Enfield says it was a man called Hyde.

beats.scene: Enfield tries to describe a man whose face he cannot explain.
beats.summary: Enfield says that Hyde is not easy to describe: there is something wrong and detestable about him, a feeling of deformity that he cannot name.

beats.scene: Utterson and Enfield shake hands on a quiet pavement.
beats.summary: Utterson asks whether Hyde really used a key and admits he knows who signed the cheque; Enfield regrets his long tongue, and they promise never to speak of it again.

beats.scene: Utterson sits at a table, eating dinner with a gloomy face.
beats.summary: That evening Utterson goes home in a sombre mood and eats without pleasure; instead of his usual dry book by the fire, he takes a candle and goes to his business room.

beats.scene: A lawyer unlocks a heavy iron safe by candlelight.
beats.summary: Utterson opens his safe and takes from its most private corner an envelope marked Dr Jekyll's Will.

beats.scene: Utterson reads a long handwritten will beneath the lamplight.
beats.summary: The will is written in Jekyll's own hand; Utterson refused to help make it, and it leaves everything to Jekyll's friend and benefactor Edward Hyde.

beats.scene: A finger rests on one line of the will beneath the candle.
beats.summary: The will adds that if Jekyll disappears or is absent for more than three months, Hyde is to take his place at once and free of every burden.

beats.scene: Utterson frowns over the will as the candle burns low.
beats.summary: The will has long been an eyesore to Utterson; while Hyde was only a name it was bad, and now that he knows something of him, it is worse.

beats.scene: Utterson puts on his coat and sets out through the lamplit streets.
beats.summary: Utterson says it was madness and he fears it is disgrace; he puts the will away and walks to Cavendish Square, where his friend Dr Lanyon lives.

beats.scene: Dr Lanyon, red-faced with white hair, greets Utterson warmly beside a dining table.
beats.summary: Lanyon, a hearty, red-faced man with prematurely white hair, welcomes Utterson with both hands; they are old school friends who truly enjoy each other's company.

beats.scene: Two old friends sit by a fire talking about a third.
beats.summary: Utterson asks Lanyon about Jekyll, and Lanyon says that for more than ten years Jekyll has been too fanciful for him and has gone wrong in his mind.

beats.scene: Utterson, in his dark bedroom, tosses beneath the curtains of a great bed.
beats.summary: Utterson, relieved that it is only a quarrel about science, asks about Hyde; Lanyon has never heard of him, and Utterson goes home to a sleepless night.

beats.scene: A faceless figure in the fog stands beside a sleeper's bed.
beats.summary: Utterson dreams of a figure without a face that tramples children and stands at Jekyll's bedside; he longs to see the real Hyde's face and decides, "If he be Mr Hyde, I shall be Mr Seek."

beats.scene: A lawyer waits beside a shabby door in the grey light of morning.
beats.summary: Utterson begins to haunt the door in the by-street, watching it in the morning before his office opens.

beats.scene: Utterson watches from the shadows under a fogged city moon.
beats.summary: He keeps watch at noon, when business is busy and time scarce, and at night under the foggy moon, at all hours and in all lights.

beats.scene: A frosty night, clean pavements and a small figure approaching the door.
beats.summary: At last, on a fine dry night with frost in the air, a light, odd footstep sounds from far off, and Utterson steps into the entry of the court.

beats.scene: A small, pale man takes out a key beside the shabby door.
beats.summary: Hyde draws near and takes out a key like a man coming home; Utterson steps out, touches his shoulder and calls him Mr Hyde, and Hyde shrinks back with a hiss.

beats.scene: Two men stand face to face at a door in the lamplight.
beats.summary: Utterson says he is an old friend of Dr Jekyll and hoped to be let in; Hyde says Jekyll is from home, then suddenly asks how Utterson knew him.

beats.scene: Hyde turns his pale face boldly towards Utterson beneath the lamp.
beats.summary: Utterson asks to see Hyde's face; after hesitating, Hyde turns with an air of defiance, and they stare at each other; Utterson says he will know him again.

beats.scene: Hyde speaks sharply and names a street in Soho.
beats.summary: Hyde agrees it is as well they have met and gives his address in Soho; Utterson wonders whether Hyde, too, has been thinking of the will.

beats.scene: Hyde snarls and laughs, then slips through the door and vanishes.
beats.summary: Hyde asks again how he was known; Utterson says Jekyll described him; Hyde cries that Jekyll never told him, then snarls with savage laughter and vanishes through the door.

beats.scene: Utterson stands alone in the empty street, gazing at the closed door.
beats.summary: Utterson stands troubled and recalls Hyde: pale, dwarfish, with a feeling of deformity, a smile, a husky whisper; none of it explains his loathing, and he thinks he has seen the sign of Satan on his face.

beats.scene: A butler holds open a grand door in a square of old houses.
beats.summary: Utterson goes round the corner to Jekyll's grand house and Poole tells him the doctor is out, that Hyde has a key, and that all the servants have been told to obey him.

beats.scene: A warm dining room where six gentlemen laugh around a candlelit table.
beats.summary: A fortnight later Jekyll gives one of his pleasant dinners for five or six old friends, all clever, respectable men and good judges of wine.

beats.scene: The guests leave and only Utterson remains by the glowing fire.
beats.summary: Utterson contrives to stay behind after the others have gone, as he often does, because Jekyll's friends like to sit with the quiet lawyer when the noise has ended.

beats.scene: Dr Jekyll, a large, smooth-faced man in his fifties, sits by the fire.
beats.summary: Jekyll is a large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty, with a slightly sly look, but every sign of ability and kindness, and a warm affection for Utterson.

beats.scene: Utterson leans forward and speaks seriously to the doctor.
beats.summary: Utterson says he has been wanting to talk; Jekyll jokes that Utterson is unlucky in such a client and says Lanyon is a hide-bound pedant about his scientific heresies.

beats.scene: The doctor's smile fades as the lawyer speaks the name of Hyde.
beats.summary: Utterson says he never approved of the will and that he has been learning something of young Hyde; Jekyll's face goes pale and dark about the eyes.

beats.scene: Jekyll holds up a hand, his face tight with distress.
beats.summary: Jekyll says he does not care to hear more; Utterson says what he heard was abominable; Jekyll answers that his position is very strange and cannot be mended by talking.

beats.scene: Jekyll holds out his hand over the fire in a firm promise.
beats.summary: Jekyll says he trusts Utterson and is quite sure he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, and he gives his hand upon it.

beats.scene: Utterson looks into the fire while Jekyll waits for an answer.
beats.summary: Jekyll adds that this is a private matter and begs Utterson to let it sleep; Utterson looks into the fire for a while, then agrees that Jekyll is probably right.

beats.scene: Jekyll lays a hand on Utterson's arm and speaks earnestly.
beats.summary: Jekyll says he takes a great interest in poor Hyde and asks Utterson to promise that, if he himself is taken away, he will bear with Hyde and get him his rights.

beats.scene: Utterson walks home alone through quiet streets, his head bent.
beats.summary: Utterson sighs and promises; he goes home uneasy, knowing that he has bound himself to help a man he fears.

beats.scene: Newspaper boys cry out in a London street at dawn.
beats.summary: Nearly a year later, in October, London is shocked by a crime of singular violence, made more notable by the high rank of the victim.

beats.scene: A maid climbs the stairs of a quiet house near the river.
beats.summary: A maid, alone in a house not far from the river, goes upstairs to bed at about eleven; the early night is clear and the lane below her window is lit by a full moon.

beats.scene: A young maid sits dreaming at her window above a moonlit lane.
beats.summary: The maid, who is romantic by nature, sits on her box beneath the window and drifts into a daydream, feeling at peace with all men.

beats.scene: An elderly gentleman with white hair walks along a bright lane.
beats.summary: She becomes aware of an aged, handsome gentleman with white hair walking along the lane, and of a very small man coming the other way to meet him.

beats.scene: The old gentleman bows politely to a small man in the moonlight.
beats.summary: The old gentleman speaks to the other with a pretty politeness, as if only asking his way; his face seems kindly and old-fashioned, and the maid is pleased to watch it.

beats.scene: Moonlight shows the small man's face, and the maid at the window recoils.
beats.summary: The maid looks at the other man and is surprised to recognise Mr Hyde, who once visited her master and whom she disliked.

beats.scene: Hyde raises a heavy cane in a sudden fury beside the old man.
beats.summary: Suddenly Hyde breaks out in a great flame of anger, stamping his foot and brandishing the cane like a madman.

beats.scene: A raised cane falls in the moonlight as the old man drops.
beats.summary: Hyde breaks out of all control and strikes the old man to the ground, then beats him with ape-like fury until he lies still; the maid faints.

beats.scene: A police officer kneels in the lane by the body of an old man.
beats.summary: At two o'clock the maid comes to herself and calls the police; the murderer is long gone, but his victim lies in the middle of the lane.

beats.scene: Police examine half a broken cane and a sealed letter in the lane.
beats.summary: The cane, of rare tough wood, has broken in the middle and one half lies in the gutter; a purse and gold watch are found on the victim, and a letter addressed to Mr Utterson.

beats.scene: A police officer hands a letter to Utterson in his bedroom.
beats.summary: Next morning, before Utterson is out of bed, a police officer brings him the letter and the news; Utterson dresses gravely and drives to the station where the body lies.

beats.scene: A lawyer looks sadly down at a covered figure in a bare room.
beats.summary: Utterson recognises the body as Sir Danvers Carew; the officer, excited at once, tells him what the maid saw and shows the broken stick.

beats.scene: Utterson stares at half a broken cane lying on a table.
beats.summary: Utterson has already quailed at the name of Hyde; he recognises the stick as one he gave to Henry Jekyll many years ago, and offers to take the officer to Hyde's house.

beats.scene: A cab crawls through thick brown fog between the lamps of London.
beats.summary: It is about nine and the first fog of the season; as the cab crawls through the streets, the lawyer sees every shade of darkness and a glow like a strange fire.

beats.scene: A grimy Soho street with a gin shop and ragged children in doorways.
beats.summary: At the address the fog lifts to show a dingy street, a gin palace, a cheap French eating house and ragged children; it is hard to believe that this is the home of Jekyll's favourite.

beats.scene: An old woman with silver hair opens a door and eyes the visitors.
beats.summary: An old woman with an evil face but excellent manners says that Hyde is out and often away; when the inspector reveals who he is, she shows odious joy and asks what Hyde has done.

beats.scene: Two men stand in a handsome room hung with a good painting.
beats.summary: Hyde uses only two rooms in the house, but they are furnished with luxury and good taste: a closet of wine, silver plate, fine linen, a good picture and soft carpets.

beats.scene: Burnt papers and torn clothes lie scattered across a lodging floor.
beats.summary: The rooms have been hurriedly ransacked, with clothes on the floor and drawers open, and the hearth holds grey ashes; the inspector finds a charred cheque-book and the other half of the cane behind a door.

beats.scene: A smiling inspector talks to Utterson outside a bank in the fog.
beats.summary: At the bank, several thousand pounds are found to Hyde's credit; the inspector says that he has Hyde in his hand, because Hyde has lost his head and money is life to him.

beats.scene: Handbills describing a small man are pasted on a foggy wall.
beats.summary: The hunt is not easy, for Hyde has few friends, no known family and no photograph, and those who describe him differ widely, though all agree on the sense of deformity.

beats.scene: Utterson crosses a foggy garden court behind a grand house.
beats.summary: That afternoon Utterson goes to Jekyll's door and Poole leads him across the old garden to the windowless block that was once a surgeon's dissecting rooms.

beats.scene: A gaunt old surgical theatre with crates, and a stair to a red door.
beats.summary: Utterson crosses the silent theatre, strewn with crates and straw, climbs a stair to a door of red baize and enters the cabinet, where Jekyll sits close to the fire, looking deadly sick.

beats.scene: Utterson asks a pale Jekyll a question beside the fire.
beats.summary: Utterson asks if Jekyll has heard the news, and whether he is mad enough to hide Hyde; Jekyll swears to God that he will never set eyes on him again.

beats.scene: Jekyll grips the arm of his chair, speaking with feverish urgency.
beats.summary: Jekyll says Hyde is safe and will never more be heard of; Utterson warns that Jekyll's name might appear at a trial, and Jekyll says he has a letter and wants advice about it.

beats.scene: Utterson holds a letter close to the lamp and reads it closely.
beats.summary: Jekyll says that he does not care what becomes of Hyde, only about his own character; Utterson, surprised at his selfishness yet relieved, asks to see the letter.

beats.scene: A short note in an odd, upright hand lies on a desk.
beats.summary: The letter is in an odd, upright hand and signed Edward Hyde; it says that his benefactor Dr Jekyll need not fear for his safety, because the writer has a sure means of escape.

beats.scene: Jekyll buries his face in his hands in the dim cabinet.
beats.summary: Jekyll burned the envelope and says the note was handed in; when Utterson asks if Hyde dictated the will's disappearance clause, Jekyll nods, and says he has had a lesson.

beats.scene: Utterson pauses in a hall to question a worried butler.
beats.summary: On the way out, Utterson asks Poole about the messenger who brought the letter; Poole says nothing came except by post, so the letter must have come through the laboratory door.

beats.scene: Utterson and his clerk sit by a bright fire with old wine.
beats.summary: That evening Utterson sits by his fire with his head clerk, Mr Guest, over a bottle of old wine, and decides to show him Hyde's letter, because Guest is a great student of handwriting.

beats.scene: A clerk holds two letters side by side under a lamp.
beats.summary: Guest studies Hyde's letter and calls it an odd hand; when a note from Jekyll arrives, he compares the two and finds them alike but differently sloped, and Utterson thinks that Jekyll has forged for a murderer.

beats.scene: Handbills offering a large reward cover a foggy London wall.
beats.summary: Thousands of pounds are offered as a reward, for the death of Sir Danvers is felt as a public injury, but Hyde has vanished from the sight of the police as if he had never existed.

beats.scene: A police officer reads a long report at a cluttered desk.
beats.summary: Much of Hyde's past is dug up, and all of it is disreputable: stories of his cruelty, his vile life, his strange companions and the hatred that followed him; but nobody knows where he is.

beats.scene: Utterson, calmer, sits at his desk in the morning light.
beats.summary: From the morning of the murder Hyde is simply blotted out; Utterson slowly recovers from his alarm and thinks that the disappearance of Hyde more than pays for the death of Sir Danvers.

beats.scene: Jekyll, smiling and at ease, welcomes friends into his bright drawing room.
beats.summary: Jekyll comes out of his seclusion, renews his friendships and becomes once more a familiar guest and host; he was always known for charity and is now as well known for religion.

beats.scene: Dr Jekyll walks briskly through a sunlit park, his face bright.
beats.summary: Jekyll is busy, much in the open air and doing good; his face seems to brighten as if he knows he is of service, and for more than two months he is at peace.

beats.scene: Three old friends laugh together around a candlelit dinner table.
beats.summary: On the eighth of January Utterson dines at the doctor's with a small party, and Lanyon is there; the host looks from one to another as in the old days when the three were inseparable friends.

beats.scene: Poole stands at a closed front door and shakes his head.
beats.summary: On the twelfth the door is shut against the lawyer, and again on the fourteenth; Poole says that the doctor is confined to the house and sees no one.

beats.scene: A lawyer stands on the steps of a house as the door closes again.
beats.summary: On the fifteenth he tries again and is refused again; used to seeing his friend almost daily for two months, he finds the return of solitude weighs upon his spirits.

beats.scene: Utterson dines at home with his clerk, Guest, in a lamplit room.
beats.summary: On the fifth night Utterson has Guest to dine with him, to keep away his gloom.

beats.scene: Utterson stands before Lanyon's tall front door in Cavendish Square.
beats.summary: On the sixth night Utterson goes to Dr Lanyon's, where at least he is not denied admittance.

beats.scene: A pale, thin doctor sits alone in a dim dining room.
beats.summary: The once rosy Lanyon is pale, thin, balder and visibly older; Utterson sees a death sentence written on his face, and in his eyes a deep terror of the mind.

beats.scene: Lanyon sits with a trembling hand upon the table.
beats.summary: Lanyon says he has had a shock from which he will never recover, that it is a question of weeks, and that life was pleasant but he would now be glad to be gone.

beats.scene: Lanyon raises a shaking hand to stop the lawyer from speaking.
beats.summary: Utterson says Jekyll is ill too and asks if Lanyon has seen him; Lanyon holds up a trembling hand and says he wishes to see or hear no more of Dr Jekyll.

beats.scene: Utterson leans forward to plead with his old friend.
beats.summary: Utterson pleads that three old friends should not part, but Lanyon says nothing can be done and that Jekyll himself must be asked; Utterson says Jekyll will not see him, and Lanyon is not surprised.

beats.scene: Two old friends sit in silence in a room lit by one lamp.
beats.summary: Lanyon says that some day after his death Utterson may learn the right and wrong of it, and asks him either to talk of other things or to go, for he cannot bear that subject.

beats.scene: Utterson writes a letter at his desk, his pen scratching in lamplight.
beats.summary: As soon as he gets home, Utterson writes to Jekyll, complaining of his exclusion from the house and asking the cause of the unhappy break with Lanyon.

beats.scene: Jekyll's answer lies unfolded on Utterson's desk beside a candle.
beats.summary: The next day Jekyll's long answer comes, pathetic and mysterious; he says the quarrel with Lanyon is incurable, that he will live in extreme seclusion, and that he has brought on himself a punishment he cannot name.

beats.scene: Utterson sits frowning at a letter, his tea gone cold.
beats.summary: Utterson is amazed: Hyde's evil influence has gone, Jekyll had returned to his old tasks, and a week ago the prospect had smiled; now friendship and peace are wrecked, which points to madness, yet Lanyon's words suggest a deeper cause.

beats.scene: Mourners in black stand in a grey churchyard beside a new grave.
beats.summary: A week later Lanyon takes to his bed and in less than a fortnight he is dead; after the funeral Utterson opens an envelope in his dead friend's hand marked for him alone.

beats.scene: Utterson locks a sealed packet into a dark iron safe.
beats.summary: Inside is another sealed enclosure, marked not to be opened until the death or disappearance of Henry Jekyll; Utterson, bound by honour, locks the packet away unopened.

beats.scene: Two men walk side by side along a quiet Sunday street.
beats.summary: It happens that on a Sunday Utterson is on his usual walk with Enfield, and their way leads again through the by-street of shops.

beats.scene: Enfield and Utterson stop in front of the shabby door.
beats.summary: They pass the door and stop; Enfield says that at least that story is at an end and they will never see Hyde again, and Utterson admits that he once met him and felt the same disgust.

beats.scene: Enfield laughs ruefully and taps his stick on the pavement.
beats.summary: Enfield says that Utterson must have thought him an ass for not knowing that this was a back way to Dr Jekyll's, and that it was partly Utterson's fault that he found out.

beats.scene: Utterson turns away from the street and looks into a gloomy court.
beats.summary: Utterson proposes that they step into the court and look at the windows, because he is uneasy about poor Jekyll and thinks that the presence of a friend might do him good even from outside.

beats.scene: A small damp courtyard lies in shadow under a bright evening sky.
beats.summary: The court is very cool and a little damp, and full of early twilight, though the sky overhead is still bright with sunset.

beats.scene: A pale man sits at a half-open window above a gloomy court.
beats.summary: The middle one of the three windows is half open, and sitting close to it, taking the air with an infinite sadness like a disconsolate prisoner, is Dr Jekyll.

beats.scene: Utterson calls up to the window while Jekyll leans on the sill.
beats.summary: Jekyll says he is very low and that it will not last long, thank God; Utterson urges him to come out for a walk, introducing his cousin Mr Enfield.

beats.scene: Jekyll shakes his head at the window, smiling faintly.
beats.summary: Jekyll says he would like it very much but dare not, and that the place is not fit for visitors; Utterson suggests that they speak from where they stand, and Jekyll smiles and agrees.

beats.scene: A smile vanishes from a face at a window, replaced by terror.
beats.summary: The words are hardly said before the smile is struck from Jekyll's face and replaced by an expression of abject terror and despair that freezes the blood of the two men; the window is thrust down.

beats.scene: Two pale men walk away in silence through a quiet street.
beats.summary: They leave the court without a word and walk in silence until they reach a living street, where they look at each other, pale and horrified, and Utterson says, God forgive us.

beats.scene: Utterson sits by his fireside after dinner as a knock sounds.
beats.summary: One evening after dinner, as Utterson sits by his fire, he is surprised by a visit from Poole and asks what is the matter.

beats.scene: A butler perches on the edge of a chair in a warm study.
beats.summary: Poole says that there is something wrong; Utterson gives him a glass of wine and tells him to take his time and say plainly what he wants.

beats.scene: Poole twists his hands together, afraid to speak.
beats.summary: Poole says that Jekyll has shut himself up in the cabinet again and that he does not like it; he has been afraid for about a week and can bear it no more.

beats.scene: Poole sits with an untouched glass of wine on his knee.
beats.summary: Poole's appearance bears out his words; he does not look Utterson in the face and leaves the wine untasted; he says he thinks there has been foul play, and asks the lawyer to come and see for himself.

beats.scene: Utterson takes his hat and greatcoat from a hook by the door.
beats.summary: Utterson only rises to fetch his hat and greatcoat, and notices with wonder the great relief on the butler's face and that the wine is still untasted.

beats.scene: A pale moon lies tilted among torn clouds over a windy street.
beats.summary: It is a wild, cold, seasonable night of March, with a pale moon lying on her back as though the wind had tilted her, and thin clouds flying across the sky.

beats.scene: A long empty street lit by a few lamps in a high wind.
beats.summary: The streets are unusually empty, and Utterson has never seen that part of London so deserted; he feels a sharp wish to touch his fellow-creatures, for a crushing sense of calamity presses on his mind.

beats.scene: Poole stops in a windy square, wiping his face with a red handkerchief.
beats.summary: In the windy square, Poole stops, takes off his hat and mops his brow, sweating with anguish rather than weariness, and says that he hopes there is nothing wrong.

beats.scene: A crowd of frightened servants huddles round a high fire in a hall.
beats.summary: The door is opened on its chain; in the bright hall all the servants stand huddled round the fire like a flock of sheep, and the housemaid and cook greet Utterson with cries of relief.

beats.scene: Poole leads Utterson through a dark back garden with a candle.
beats.summary: Utterson complains that this is irregular and unseemly, but the servants say they are afraid; Poole silences the maid, takes a candle, and leads the way to the back garden, telling Utterson not to go in if Hyde asks him.

beats.scene: Two men stand at the foot of a stair inside a lumber-filled theatre.
beats.summary: Poole leads Utterson into the old theatre, among crates and straw, to the foot of the stair; he strikes the cabinet door and calls that Mr Utterson wishes to see him, and a complaining voice answers that it can see no one.

beats.scene: Poole whispers fiercely to Utterson beside the stair.
beats.summary: Poole asks if that was his master's voice; Utterson says it seems changed; Poole says that after twenty years he is not deceived, and that his master was made away with eight days ago.

beats.scene: Utterson bites his finger, thinking, in the flickering candlelight.
beats.summary: Utterson calls it a wild tale and asks what could make a murderer stay in the room; Poole says he will satisfy him yet.

beats.scene: Notes on slips of paper lie scattered at the foot of a stair.
beats.summary: For the last week, Poole says, whatever lives in the cabinet has cried night and day for a medicine and cannot get it to his mind; he leaves orders on paper on the stair, and Poole has gone to every chemist in town.

beats.scene: Utterson reads a crumpled note by candlelight.
beats.summary: Every time Poole brought the drug back, a new paper said it was not pure, and another order sent him to a different firm; Poole hands over a crumpled note to Messrs Maw begging for some of the old.

beats.scene: Utterson holds the note up and examines the handwriting.
beats.summary: Utterson asks how Poole came to have the note open, and Poole says the man at Maw's threw it back at him; it is unquestionably the doctor's hand, says Utterson, but Poole says that he has seen him.

beats.scene: A masked figure darts between crates in a dim laboratory.
beats.summary: Poole tells how he came suddenly into the theatre from the garden and found the figure digging among the crates; it gave a kind of cry and whipped upstairs into the cabinet, and its face was covered with a mask.

beats.scene: Utterson frowns as Poole whispers about a smaller figure.
beats.summary: Utterson suggests that Jekyll is seized with some disease that disfigures and changes the voice, which would explain the mask and the drug; Poole turns pale and says that the thing was not his master, who is tall, while this was more of a dwarf.

beats.scene: Poole raises a trembling hand, certain of what he says.
beats.summary: Poole says he knows where his master's head comes in the cabinet door after twenty years, and that murder has been done; Utterson says it is his duty to break in the door, and Poole offers to help.

beats.scene: Utterson balances an iron poker while Poole holds a heavy axe.
beats.summary: Poole fetches an axe and Utterson takes a poker; they admit that both of them suspect the masked figure was Hyde, and Utterson believes that poor Harry is killed and that his murderer lurks in his room.

beats.scene: Utterson gives orders to two nervous servants holding thick sticks.
beats.summary: Utterson calls the footman Bradshaw and tells him that he and Poole will force the cabinet door; Bradshaw and the boy are to guard the laboratory door with sticks, and ten minutes are given to reach their posts.

beats.scene: Two men wait in the dark theatre by a flickering candle.
beats.summary: Utterson looks at his watch and goes with Poole to the yard; the wind tosses the candle light, and they wait in the shelter of the theatre.

beats.scene: Poole listens, head tilted, toward a door at the top of a stair.
beats.summary: Nearer at hand, the silence is broken only by a footfall moving to and fro along the cabinet floor; Poole whispers that it will walk all day and the better part of the night.

beats.scene: Poole puts a finger to his lips and points up the stairs.
beats.summary: Poole asks Utterson to put his heart in his ears and say if it is the doctor's foot; the steps fall lightly and oddly with a certain swing, very different from Jekyll's heavy creaking tread.

beats.scene: A lawyer shivers in the dark, listening to a distant sound.
beats.summary: Utterson asks if there was ever anything else; Poole says that once he heard it weeping, like a woman or a lost soul, and came away with a heart so heavy that he could have wept too.

beats.scene: Poole pulls an axe from a pile of straw as Utterson stands by.
beats.summary: The ten minutes end; Poole digs out the axe from under packing straw, sets the candle on a table, and they approach the stairs; Utterson calls to Jekyll that he demands to see him, by force if necessary.

beats.scene: A voice cries out from behind a locked red door.
beats.summary: A voice answers, begging Utterson for God's sake to have mercy; Utterson knows at once that it is not Jekyll's voice but Hyde's, and orders Poole to break down the door.

beats.scene: Poole swings the axe at a red baize door in the lamplight.
beats.summary: Poole swings the axe and the blow shakes the building; a dismal screech of animal terror rings from the cabinet, and the axe falls four times, but the wood is tough.

beats.scene: A broken door opens onto a quiet room with a fire and a kettle.
beats.summary: At the fifth blow the lock bursts and the door falls inwards; the two men, appalled by their own riot and the stillness that follows, peer in and see a quiet room with a good fire, a singing kettle and tea things laid out.

beats.scene: A small man lies still on a carpet in clothes too large.
beats.summary: In the middle of the floor lies a man, who proves to be Edward Hyde, dressed in clothes too large for him and holding a crushed phial; Utterson knows from the smell that Hyde has taken his own life.

beats.scene: Two men with a candle search a dusty corridor and an empty closet.
beats.summary: Utterson says they are too late to save or punish and that they must find Jekyll's body; they search the whole building, theatre, closets and cellar, but every closet is empty and a mat of cobweb seals the cellar.

beats.scene: Poole stamps on the stone floor of a long corridor.
beats.summary: There is no trace of Henry Jekyll, dead or alive; Poole stamps on the flags and says that he must be buried there, but Utterson thinks he may have fled and goes to look at the door in the by-street.

beats.scene: A broken rusty key lies on the stone floor by a locked door.
beats.summary: The door is locked, and near it on the flags lies the key, already stained with rust and broken in two, as if a man had stamped on it; the fractures are rusty too, and the two men look at each other in alarm.

beats.scene: Glass saucers hold small heaps of white salt on a work table.
beats.summary: In the cabinet they find traces of chemical work, with measured heaps of white salt on glass saucers as if for an experiment that the unhappy man was prevented from finishing; Poole says it is the drug he was always bringing, and the kettle boils over.

beats.scene: An armchair stands by the fire with tea things laid ready.
beats.summary: At the fireside the easy-chair is drawn up cosily with the tea things ready to the sitter's elbow, and beside them lies a pious book that Jekyll admired, marked in his own hand with shocking blasphemies.

beats.scene: Two pale faces look into a tall mirror that reflects only firelight.
beats.summary: They come to the tall mirror and look into its depths with horror, but it is turned so as to show only the glow of the fire on the ceiling and their own pale, frightened faces; Poole whispers that it has seen strange things.

beats.scene: A thick envelope with Utterson's name lies on a tidy desk.
beats.summary: On the business table, among the neat papers, a large envelope bears Utterson's name; inside is a will in the same strange terms as the old one, but with Utterson's name in place of Hyde's.

beats.scene: Utterson stares from the paper to the body on the carpet.
beats.summary: Utterson says his head goes round, because Hyde was in possession for days and has not destroyed this document; a second paper, a dated note, tells him that Jekyll was alive that very day, and he fears they must be careful.

beats.scene: Utterson holds a short note beneath the lamp, reading with dread.
beats.summary: Utterson fears to read the note; when he does, Jekyll says that when it falls into Utterson's hands he will have disappeared, and tells him to read Lanyon's narrative first, and then the confession of his unhappy friend.

beats.scene: Utterson slips a thick sealed packet into his coat pocket.
beats.summary: Poole hands over a third enclosure, a thick packet sealed in several places; Utterson puts it in his pocket, tells Poole to say nothing, and promises to return before midnight to send for the police.

beats.scene: Utterson reads Lanyon's letter by his fireside at night.
beats.summary: Utterson goes home, takes Lanyon's packet from his safe, and reads: a registered envelope in Jekyll's hand had reached Lanyon by the evening post, though he had dined with Jekyll the night before.

beats.scene: A trembling hand holds a letter that begs for help.
beats.summary: Jekyll's letter says that Lanyon is one of his oldest friends and that his life, honour and reason are at his mercy; if Lanyon fails him tonight, he is lost.

beats.scene: A doctor reads instructions by lamplight at his dining table.
beats.summary: Jekyll begs Lanyon to put aside all other engagements, take a cab to his house, where Poole will be waiting with a locksmith, force the door of the cabinet, and take out the fourth drawer from the top of the glazed press marked E.

beats.scene: A drawer holds powders, a glass phial and a paper book.
beats.summary: Lanyon is to open the glazed press marked E, breaking the lock if necessary, take out the fourth drawer from the top with all its contents, some powders, a phial and a paper book, and carry it back to Cavendish Square exactly as it stands.

beats.scene: A clock shows midnight over a quiet doctor's consulting room.
beats.summary: Then comes the second part: at midnight Lanyon must be alone in his consulting room, admit with his own hand a man who will present himself in Jekyll's name, and put the drawer into his hands; neglect of any step might cost Jekyll his life or his reason.

beats.scene: A postscript is scrawled in a hasty hand at the foot of a page.
beats.summary: Jekyll writes that his troubles will roll away like a story that is told if Lanyon serves him; in a postscript he adds that, if the post is late, Lanyon must still expect his messenger at midnight, and that if the night passes without event, Lanyon will have seen the last of Henry Jekyll.

beats.scene: Lanyon puts down the letter and reaches for his hat in alarm.
beats.summary: Lanyon decides that his colleague is insane, but until it is proved he feels bound to do as he is asked; he leaves his dinner, takes a cab and drives straight to Jekyll's house.

beats.scene: A locksmith and a carpenter stand with Poole before a heavy door.
beats.summary: Poole is waiting with a registered letter of the same instructions, and has sent for a locksmith and a carpenter; they all go to old Dr Denman's theatre, where the door of the cabinet is very strong.

beats.scene: A door swings open and a doctor carries a drawer wrapped in a sheet.
beats.summary: The locksmith is a handy fellow, and after two hours' work the door stands open; Lanyon finds the press marked E unlocked, takes out the drawer, fills it with straw, ties it in a sheet and carries it home to Cavendish Square.

beats.scene: A doctor opens a wrapper to find a white crystalline salt.
beats.summary: Lanyon examines the drawer: the powders are not made up as neatly as a dispensing chemist would do, so they are of Jekyll's own making; one wrapper holds a white crystalline salt, and the phial is half full of a blood-red liquid with a sharp smell.

beats.scene: A doctor turns the pages of a notebook filled with dates.
beats.summary: The book is an ordinary notebook with a series of dates over many years that ceased abruptly nearly a year ago; here and there is a word such as double, and once, early on, total failure with exclamation marks.

beats.scene: A doctor loads an old revolver beside a desk at night.
beats.summary: Lanyon cannot see how these things could touch the honour, sanity or life of his flighty colleague, and concludes he is dealing with brain disease; he sends his servants to bed and loads an old revolver so as to be ready.

beats.scene: A small man crouches against the pillars of a doorway at midnight.
beats.summary: Hardly have the bells of London rung out midnight when a gentle knock sounds; Lanyon finds a small man crouching against the pillars of the portico, who answers by a gesture that he comes from Jekyll, and glances fearfully backwards.

beats.scene: A pale small stranger blinks in the bright light of a doctor's study.
beats.summary: Lanyon keeps his hand on his weapon as he follows the man into the light; he has never set eyes on him before, and notes his shocking face, his strange mixture of strength and weakness and the odd disturbance caused by his presence.

beats.scene: A very small man stands in clothes that hang loose on every limb.
beats.summary: The visitor is dressed in a way that would have made an ordinary person laughable: his clothes are of good cloth but enormously too large, the trousers rolled up and the collar sprawling over his shoulders, yet Lanyon feels no wish to laugh.

beats.scene: A small man grips a doctor's arm in desperate impatience.
beats.summary: The stranger cries out, asking whether Lanyon has got it, and in his impatience lays a hand on his arm; Lanyon feels an icy pang along his blood, puts him back, and tells him to be seated.

beats.scene: The stranger presses a hand to his throat, struggling for composure.
beats.summary: The man apologises civilly, says his impatience has shown its heels to his politeness, and says he comes from Jekyll on business of some moment; but he stops, hand at his throat, wrestling with hysteria.

beats.scene: A small man leaps at a drawer on the floor, then freezes.
beats.summary: Lanyon takes pity on his suspense and points to the drawer on the floor behind a table; the stranger springs to it, then pauses with his hand on his heart, his teeth grinding and his face so ghastly that Lanyon fears for his life.

beats.scene: A small man smiles dreadfully and pulls a white sheet from a drawer.
beats.summary: The stranger turns a dreadful smile to Lanyon, plucks away the sheet and sobs with great relief; he asks for a graduated glass, measures out a few drops of the red tincture, adds one of the powders, and the mixture changes colour, fizzes and smokes.

beats.scene: A small man drinks from a glass as a doctor staggers back.
beats.summary: The stranger gives Lanyon a choice, to be wise and let him go, or to see a new province of knowledge; Lanyon, curious, says he will see the end; the man drinks, reels, changes, and there stands Henry Jekyll.

beats.scene: A letter ends in a firm signature as a shaken lawyer looks up.
beats.summary: Lanyon ends his letter: he cannot set down what Jekyll told him in the next hour; his life is shaken, he will die incredulous, and the creature who crept into his house was, on Jekyll's own confession, Hyde, the murderer of Carew.

beats.scene: Utterson, grey-faced, breaks the seals of a thick packet at his desk.
beats.summary: Utterson sits in silence, then opens Jekyll's sealed packet; Jekyll begins by saying that he was born to a large fortune, with good gifts, a liking for work and a wish to be respected, though cursed with an impatient gaiety.

beats.scene: A well-dressed man shuts a door on one life and opens another.
beats.summary: Jekyll says that he hid his pleasures; by the time he took stock of his life, he was committed to a deep duplicity; yet he was no hypocrite, for both sides of him were in dead earnest.

beats.scene: A scholar bent over a book at night, seeing a truth that frightens him.
beats.summary: Jekyll's studies lead towards the mystic and the transcendental, and he comes to the truth by which he is doomed: that man is not truly one, but truly two.

beats.scene: A man dreams by a window of two figures walking apart.
beats.summary: Jekyll had long dreamed of separating the two natures, so that the unjust might go his way free of remorse and the just might walk upward unharmed; it was the curse of mankind that the two were bound together.

beats.scene: A lamp burns late in a laboratory full of glass bottles.
beats.summary: In his laboratory Jekyll finds that a certain drug can shake and change the body, like a wind tossing the curtain of a tent; he knows it is dangerous, but the temptation of so singular a discovery overcomes his fear.

beats.scene: A man holds a glowing glass in a dark laboratory at night.
beats.summary: Jekyll had long prepared his tincture and bought a large quantity of a particular salt from a firm of chemists, knowing it to be the last ingredient; on one accursed night he mixed the elements, watched them boil and smoke, and drank the potion with a strong glow of courage.

beats.scene: A man doubles over in pain, then rises with a strange new smile.
beats.summary: Racking pangs follow: a grinding in the bones, deadly nausea and a horror of the spirit; then the pain fades and Jekyll feels younger, lighter and happier, with a heady recklessness and a freedom of the soul that is not innocent.

beats.scene: A small figure stares at his reflection in a mirror at dawn.
beats.summary: Jekyll knows at the first breath of this new life that he is tenfold more wicked, and the thought delights him like wine; he creeps to his bedroom and sees for the first time the face of Edward Hyde, smaller, slighter and younger than Jekyll.

beats.scene: A small man stands before a mirror, nodding, then drinks again from a cup.
beats.summary: Jekyll feels no horror at the ugly face, only a leap of welcome, for this too is himself; he sees that others shrink from Hyde, who is pure evil; he then drinks the cup again and returns to the shape of Henry Jekyll.

beats.scene: A man stands at a dark crossroads in a laboratory, glass in hand.
beats.summary: Jekyll says that he came that night to the fatal crossroads: the drug was neither good nor evil but only shook the doors of the prison of his nature, and since his virtue slept and his evil was awake, what came forth was Edward Hyde.

beats.scene: A man in a heavy cloak looks at his reflection with a thoughtful smile.
beats.summary: Jekyll now has two characters, one wholly evil and the other the old Henry Jekyll, and the movement is wholly towards the worse; as an ageing and respected man he tires of dignity, and the new power tempts him like a thick cloak he can put on at will.

beats.scene: A small, shabby house in Soho, with a silent old housekeeper at the door.
beats.summary: Jekyll prepares with great care: he takes and furnishes the house in Soho and engages a silent, unscrupulous housekeeper; he tells his servants that a Mr Hyde is to have full liberty at his house in the square, and makes himself a familiar figure in his second character.

beats.scene: A will lies on a table beside a mirror and a tall glass.
beats.summary: Jekyll draws up the will, so that if anything happens to him as Dr Jekyll, he can become Edward Hyde without losing money; he is the first man to hire himself as the villain of his pleasures, and he feels completely safe, for Hyde can vanish like breath on a mirror.

beats.scene: Doctor Jekyll stands aghast in his study, shadows of a stranger behind him.
beats.summary: The pleasures he sought as Hyde were undignified but soon turned monstrous; Hyde was a being inherently evil, drinking pleasure from the pain of others, and Jekyll was at times aghast at his acts, but his conscience slept because Hyde alone was guilty.

beats.scene: A girl lies in a lamplit street while a small man walks away.
beats.summary: One accident he will mention: an act of cruelty to a child roused the anger of a passer-by, whom he later recognised as Utterson's kinsman; to calm the crowd, Hyde had to pay them by a cheque in Jekyll's name, so Jekyll opened an account in Hyde's name, writing his signature with his own hand sloped backward.

beats.scene: A bed in a tall room, and a dark hairy hand on the cover.
beats.summary: About two months before the murder of Sir Danvers, Jekyll woke in his own bed in the square with odd sensations; looking at his hand, which should have been large, white and comely, he saw one lean, corded, dusky and hairy, the hand of Edward Hyde.

beats.scene: A small man in baggy clothes hurries through a morning house, a footman staring.
beats.summary: Jekyll stared at it in wonder, then terror, and rushed to the mirror; he had gone to bed Henry Jekyll and awakened Edward Hyde; all his drugs were in the cabinet across the court, but the servants were used to his second self, and Bradshaw stared as he passed, and ten minutes later Jekyll sat at breakfast.

beats.scene: Jekyll sits alone before an untouched breakfast, staring at nothing.
beats.summary: Jekyll sees the accident as a warning that he is losing hold of his better self and being slowly merged with the worse; he must choose between the two, and as most tempted sinners do, he chooses the better part, bids farewell to Hyde's liberty and youth, but keeps the house in Soho and Hyde's clothes.

beats.scene: A caged beast paces behind iron bars in a dim cellar.
beats.summary: For two months Jekyll lived with great severity and enjoyed the reward of an approving conscience; then his alarm faded, he was tormented by longings as of Hyde struggling after freedom, and in an hour of moral weakness he mixed and swallowed the draught again, and his devil, long caged, came out roaring.

beats.scene: A raised cane in a moonlit lane, the shadow of a fallen old man.
beats.summary: Jekyll wrote that his caged devil came out roaring, and that he listened to the politeness of his victim with a storm of impatience; no sane man could have committed the crime on so small a provocation, and he struck like a sick child breaking a toy.

beats.scene: A small man runs through dark streets with a song on his lips.
beats.summary: When weariness came, Hyde was struck through the heart by a thrill of terror; he saw that he had forfeited his life, fled to the house in Soho, burned his papers, and walked through the lamplit streets gloating over his crime and listening for the avenger.

beats.scene: A man kneels on a floor, hands clasped, tears on his face.
beats.summary: The pangs of transformation had not finished with Hyde before Jekyll fell upon his knees with tears of gratitude and remorse and lifted his clasped hands to God; the veil of self-indulgence was torn away, and he saw his life as a whole, from childhood to that horror.

beats.scene: A man grinds a small key under his heel in a back-street doorway.
beats.summary: Jekyll shut the door of the by-street and ground the key under his heel; the next day he learned that the murder had been witnessed and that the victim was a man high in public esteem, so that Jekyll was now his city of refuge, and he resolved to redeem the past.

beats.scene: A man on a park bench in winter sun stares at his hand.
beats.summary: One fine clear January day, as Jekyll sat on a bench in Regent's Park, content and comparing himself with other men, a qualm came over him; his clothes hung loose on his shrunken limbs and his hand was corded and hairy, and he was once more Edward Hyde, hunted and houseless.

beats.scene: A hunted small man gnaws his nails by a hotel fire.
beats.summary: A moment before he had been safe and beloved; now he was the common quarry of mankind, hunted, houseless and a known murderer; he took a room in a hotel in Portland Street, wrote two letters, to Lanyon and to Poole, and had them registered.

beats.scene: A shaken man wakes in his own bed and sighs with relief.
beats.summary: After the scene at Lanyon's, Jekyll came home and slept deeply; he woke shaken but refreshed, grateful to be at home and near his drugs, but while crossing the court after breakfast the shudder came again, and he needed a double dose to return to himself.

beats.scene: An exhausted man sits awake in a chair, afraid to close his eyes.
beats.summary: From that day it seemed that only by a great effort and with the drug could Jekyll wear his own face; if he slept even a moment in his chair, he woke as Hyde; he became feverish, weak and consumed by the horror of his other self.

beats.scene: A near-empty bottle of white salt stands beside a pen in the lamplight.
beats.summary: Jekyll and Hyde hated each other equally; then the last calamity came: the supply of salt ran low, the fresh supply did not work, London was searched in vain, and Jekyll concluded that his first supply had been impure; he is finishing the statement under the last of the old powders.

beats.scene: A lone candle burns beside a finished letter and a sealed envelope.
beats.summary: About a week has passed and Jekyll finishes his statement under the last of the old powders; it is the last time he can think his own thoughts or see his own face; he does not know whether Hyde will die on the scaffold or find the courage to end it himself, and he brings the life of Henry Jekyll to an end.

A1A2: Mr Utterson was a London lawyer with a plain face and a serious manner.
He drank plain gin alone and had not seen a play for twenty years.
Every Sunday he walked with his cousin, Mr Enfield, through the city.
One Sunday they walked into a small street full of bright shops.
There stood an ugly old house with no windows and one dirty door.
Enfield pointed his stick at the door and said it had a strange story.
Once, at three on a dark winter morning, he was walking home alone.
Then he saw a small man walking fast, and a girl running.
The man knocked the girl down and walked calmly over her.
Enfield shouted, ran after the man, and caught him by the coat.
The girl's family came, and a doctor came, and everyone looked angry.
The man said coldly, “Name your price, and I will pay.”
He led them to this very door, opened it, and went in.
Enfield did not trust the cheque, so he kept the man close.
At the bank, a clerk looked at the cheque and said it was good.
Enfield said, “I call that place Black Mail House.”
Enfield never asked about the house, but he had watched it.
Utterson asked the man's name, and Enfield said, “Hyde.”
Enfield said there was something wrong with the man's look.
They shook hands and promised never to speak of it again.
That night Utterson ate his dinner with a heavy heart.
He opened his safe and took out a paper marked Dr Jekyll's Will.
Dr Jekyll had written it himself, and it left everything to Hyde.
If the doctor vanished for three months, Hyde would take everything.
The will had always troubled him, and now it troubled him more.
He walked to the house of Dr Lanyon, an old friend.
Dr Lanyon was happy to see Utterson, his old school friend.
Lanyon said Jekyll's ideas had become strange ten years ago.
Lanyon had never heard of Hyde, so Utterson went home.
In his dream, a man with no face walked through the city.
Every morning before work, Utterson stood by the shabby door.
He came at noon, and he came again at night.
At last, on a cold, clear night, he heard small footsteps.
A small man came to the door and took out a key.
Utterson said he was a friend of Dr Jekyll.
Utterson asked to see his face, and Hyde turned around.
Hyde gave an address in Soho, and Utterson wondered why.
Hyde laughed in an ugly way and went inside quickly.
Utterson stood still, and he felt cold and afraid.
Poole said that Hyde had a key and the servants must obey.
Two weeks later, Dr Jekyll gave a dinner for his old friends.
When the guests left, Utterson stayed behind with his friend.
Jekyll was a big man of fifty with a kind face.
Utterson said he wished to talk, and Jekyll smiled.
When Utterson spoke of Hyde, Jekyll's face went pale.
“This matter cannot be fixed by talking,” said Jekyll.
Jekyll said he could be free of Hyde whenever he wished.
Jekyll asked him to let the matter sleep, and Utterson agreed.
Jekyll asked Utterson to help Hyde if he was gone.
Utterson sighed deeply and said, “Well, I promise.”
A year later, London heard of a terrible crime.
A maid went up to bed at eleven o'clock.
She sat at her window and dreamed in the moonlight.
She saw an old man with white hair walking slowly.
The old man bowed and spoke very politely to the small man.
Then she looked at the small man and knew his face.
Suddenly Hyde stamped his foot and shook his heavy cane.
Hyde struck the old man down, and the maid fainted.
At two o'clock she woke up and called the police.
The police found a broken cane and a letter for Utterson.
A police officer came to Utterson's house early the next morning.
Utterson looked and said, “This is Sir Danvers Carew.”
Utterson knew the cane, because he had given it to Jekyll.
The cab moved slowly through the first thick fog of winter.
The street was poor and dirty, with ragged children in doorways.
An old woman opened the door and said Hyde was not home.
Hyde used two rooms, and they were rich and beautiful.
Hyde's rooms were a mess, and papers had been burned.
At the bank, the inspector found that Hyde had much money.
No one knew where Hyde was, and nobody could describe him.
That afternoon, Poole led Utterson through the garden to the old laboratory.
In a warm room, Jekyll sat by the fire, looking very ill.
Jekyll swore he would never see Hyde again.
Jekyll said Hyde was safe, and he showed a letter.
Jekyll said he only cared about his good name.
The letter said Hyde had a way to escape.
Jekyll nodded sadly and said, “I have learned a lesson.”
Poole said no letter had come by hand that day.
That night Utterson sat with his clerk, Mr Guest, and wine.
Guest compared the two letters and said the writing was alike.
A big reward was offered, but Hyde could not be found.
People learned many bad things about Hyde's life.
Slowly, Utterson felt calmer, and his fear began to fade.
Dr Jekyll came out of his house and met his friends again.
For two months, Dr Jekyll was busy, happy and at peace.
On January eighth, Utterson dined with Jekyll and Lanyon.
On January twelfth, Poole said Jekyll would see no one.
On the fifteenth, he tried again, but was refused again.
On the fifth night, Utterson asked Guest to dine with him.

Jekyll began, “I was born rich, and I wanted to be respected.”

One night, Jekyll mixed the drug and drank it.
There was terrible pain, and then he felt young and free.
In the mirror, he saw a small, young man with an evil face.
Then he drank again and became Henry Jekyll once more.
The drug was not good or bad, and evil came out.
Jekyll could now put on a second self like a cloak.

Jekyll made a will so that Hyde could have his money.
Hyde's pleasures became cruel, and Jekyll was afraid.
Jekyll opened a bank account in the name of Hyde.

He ran to the laboratory, drank the potion, and became Jekyll again.

Hyde killed Sir Danvers over a very small thing.

As Jekyll again, he fell on his knees and wept with shame.
Jekyll locked the back door and broke the key.
On a park bench, he felt sick and became Hyde.
Hyde went to a hotel and wrote two letters.
At home, he felt safe, but the change came again.
