Jekyll signed his name and sealed his last letter.
B1B2: Mr Utterson was a London lawyer with a rough, plain face that hardly ever smiled. He was cold in speech and awkward in company, yet something kind shone out of his eyes after a good dinner.
Dining alone, Utterson drank gin to punish his taste for fine wine, and he had not seen a play for twenty years. Yet he was always gentle and forgiving about the faults of other men.

Utterson's friends were mostly men he had known for years, and the closest was his distant cousin, Mr Enfield. Every Sunday afternoon the two walked together through London, although they seemed to have nothing in common.
One Sunday their walk took them down a narrow by-street in a busy part of London. Even on a day of rest, the shops there shone like a row of smiling salesmen.

Two doors from the corner, a gloomy block of building pushed its gable out into the street. It had no windows, only a blistered, discoloured door that had neither bell nor knocker, and it was plain that nobody cared for it.
Enfield stopped suddenly, raised his walking stick and pointed at the shabby door. He asked whether Utterson had ever noticed it, and said it was connected in his mind with a very odd story.
Enfield said he had once been coming home from the far end of town at three o'clock on a black winter morning. His way led through a quarter of the city where nothing could be seen but lamps.
Suddenly he saw two figures: a small man walking briskly east, and a girl of about eight running down a cross street. Naturally, the two of them reached the corner at the very same moment.
The man ran straight into the child and knocked her to the ground. Then, without a glance, he stepped calmly over her body and went on, leaving her screaming in the road.
Enfield gave a loud shout and ran after the stranger. He seized him by the collar and dragged him back to where the poor child was lying.
Soon the girl's family arrived, and then the doctor who had been sent for. The doctor turned white with anger whenever he looked at the stranger, who stood there cold and sneering.
The man said that he was helpless if they wished to make money out of an accident, and that no gentleman liked a scene. They named a hundred pounds for the family, and he agreed at once.
The man led the group to this very door and opened it with a key. He soon came back with ten pounds in gold and a cheque for the rest, signed with a name that Enfield will not tell.
Enfield did not like the look of it, so he said he would keep the man with them until the bank opened. The doctor, the man and Enfield went to his rooms, and they all waited there until morning.
At the bank, Enfield handed in the cheque himself and said he had every reason to think it a forgery. To his surprise, the clerk looked at it carefully and told him that it was perfectly genuine.
Enfield said that the man was detestable, while the person who signed the cheque was a famous, respectable gentleman. He supposed it was blackmail, and so he called the building Black Mail House.

Enfield said he never asked questions about such things, because one question starts others, like a stone rolling down a hill. He had watched the house, though, and noticed three clean windows and a chimney that smoked.
After some silence, Utterson said that Enfield's rule was a good one. Then he asked for the name of the man who had walked over the child, and Enfield told him it was Hyde.
Enfield found Hyde hard to describe, because something about him was wrong and quite detestable. He felt sure the man was deformed somewhere, yet he could not name a single fault.
Utterson asked whether Hyde had really used a key, and then admitted that he knew the name on the cheque. Enfield said he was ashamed of his long tongue, and they promised never to speak of it again.
That evening Utterson went home in a gloomy mood and ate his dinner without any pleasure. Instead of his usual dull book by the fire, he picked up a candle and went to his business room.
Utterson unlocked the safe and took from its most private corner an envelope marked Dr Jekyll's Will. Then he sat down with a clouded face to study what was inside.
Dr Jekyll had written the will in his own hand, because Utterson had refused to help with it. In the event of the doctor's death, everything was to pass to his friend and benefactor, Edward Hyde.

The will also said that if Dr Jekyll disappeared, or was missing for more than three months, Hyde was to take his place at once. Nothing was asked of Hyde except a few small payments to the doctor's servants.

The will had long been an eyesore to the lawyer, because it offended both his profession and his love of what was sane and ordinary. While Hyde was only a name, it was bad enough, but now it was far worse.
Utterson said to himself that he had thought it madness, but now he feared it was disgrace. He locked the will away, put on his coat and walked to Cavendish Square, where Dr Lanyon lived.
Dr Lanyon was a hearty, red-faced man with white hair and a loud, cheerful manner. He sprang up from his wine and welcomed Utterson with both hands, because they had been friends since school.
Utterson asked whether they were Jekyll's oldest friends, and Lanyon said they probably were. He added that for over ten years Jekyll had gone wrong in his mind, and that he rarely saw him now.
Utterson was relieved to hear that it was only a quarrel about science. When he asked about Hyde, however, Lanyon said he had never heard of him, and so the lawyer went home and could not sleep.
All night Enfield's story passed before his eyes, and he saw a figure with no face trampling a child. By morning he was determined to see the real Hyde, saying that if Hyde hid, he would seek.
From that day on, Mr Utterson began to haunt the door in the by-street. Each morning before his office opened, he stood in its shadow and watched.
He came at noon, when his work was heavy and his time was short, and again at night beneath the foggy moon. By every kind of light, at every hour of the day, the lawyer was found at his post.
At last his patience was rewarded, on a fine dry night with frost in the air. A light, odd footstep sounded in the distance, and Utterson stepped back into the entry of the court.

The footsteps drew quickly nearer, and a small, plainly dressed man turned into the street with a key in his hand. Utterson touched his shoulder and said, “Mr Hyde, I think,” and the man shrank back with a hissing breath.
Utterson explained that he was an old friend of Dr Jekyll's and hoped to be let in. Hyde answered that Jekyll was not at home, and then he suddenly asked how Utterson knew him.
Utterson asked Hyde to do him a favour and let him see his face. Hyde hesitated, then turned round with a look of defiance, and they stared at each other for several seconds.
Hyde said that it was as well they had met, and that Utterson ought to have his address. He named a street in Soho, and Utterson wondered whether Hyde had been thinking about the will.

When Utterson said that Jekyll was the friend who had described him, Hyde cried out angrily that Jekyll would never have told him. Then he gave a savage laugh, unlocked the door and disappeared with astonishing speed.

Utterson stood in the street for some time, deeply troubled and afraid. Hyde was pale and small, with an unpleasant smile and a whispering voice, but none of this could explain the loathing that Utterson felt.
Round the corner stood Dr Jekyll's fine house, and Utterson knocked at the door. Poole told him that the doctor was out, that Mr Hyde had a key, and that all the servants must obey him.
About a fortnight later, Dr Jekyll gave one of his pleasant little dinners to five or six old friends. They were all clever, respectable men, and every one of them was a good judge of wine.
When the other guests had gone, Utterson stayed behind, as he had often done before. Jekyll's friends liked to sit with the quiet lawyer once the noisy part of the evening was over.

Dr Jekyll was a large, well-made man of about fifty, with a smooth face and perhaps a slightly sly look. Still, every line of his face showed intelligence and kindness, and he felt real warmth towards Utterson.
Utterson said that he had long wanted to speak about the will. Jekyll joked that Utterson was unlucky in such a client, and that Lanyon, a stiff old pedant, was just as shocked by his science.

Utterson said that he had never approved of the will, and then he added that he had been learning something of young Hyde. Jekyll's large, handsome face went pale to the very lips, and a blackness came about his eyes.

Jekyll said that he did not wish to hear more, as he had thought they had agreed to drop the matter. When Utterson said what he had heard was abominable, Jekyll replied that his position was very strange and could not be mended by talking.
Jekyll said that Utterson was a man to be trusted, and that he could get rid of Hyde the moment he chose. He gave the lawyer his hand upon it and thanked him again and again.
Jekyll added that this was a private matter, and he begged Utterson to let it sleep. Utterson looked into the fire for a little while and then said that the doctor was no doubt perfectly right.
Jekyll said that he took a very great interest in poor Hyde, and he asked Utterson to promise something. If Jekyll were taken away, Utterson must bear with Hyde and see that he got his rights.
Utterson heaved a deep sigh and, after a moment, he promised to help Hyde. Then he walked home through the quiet streets, uneasy at having agreed to protect a man he feared.
Nearly a year later, in the month of October, London was startled by a crime of singular fierceness. It was made all the more shocking by the high rank of the victim.
A maid who lived alone in a house near the river went upstairs to bed at about eleven. Although a fog came later, the early night was cloudless, and a full moon lit the lane below her window.
She was a romantic girl, and instead of going to bed she sat on her box beneath the window. She fell into a dream, feeling more at peace with everyone than she had ever felt before.
As she sat there, she noticed a handsome old gentleman with white hair coming along the lane. Another man, very small, was walking towards him from the other direction.

The old gentleman bowed and spoke with a very pretty politeness, and from his pointing he seemed only to be asking the way. The moon shone on his kind, old-fashioned face, and the girl was pleased to watch it.
Presently her eye wandered to the other man, and she was surprised to recognise Mr Hyde. He had once visited her master, and she had disliked him at once.
Then, quite suddenly, Hyde broke out in a great blaze of anger. He stamped his foot and waved the cane, behaving, as the maid said, like a madman.
Hyde lost all control and struck the old man to the ground. He went on striking him with terrible fury until the man lay still, and at the sight the maid fainted.
It was two o'clock when the maid came to herself and called for the police. The murderer had been gone for a long time, but his victim lay in the middle of the lane.
The cane had snapped in the middle, and one splintered half lay in the gutter. The victim still had his purse and gold watch, together with a sealed letter addressed to Mr Utterson.
The next morning, before Utterson was out of bed, a police officer came to his house with the letter and the news. Utterson dressed with a grave face and drove at once to the police station.
Utterson looked at the dead man and said sadly that it was Sir Danvers Carew. The officer's eyes lit up, and he told Utterson what the maid had seen and showed him the broken stick.
Utterson had already turned pale at the name of Hyde, and when he saw the stick, he could doubt no longer. It was one that he had given to Henry Jekyll many years before.
It was about nine in the morning, and the first fog of the season hung over London like a great brown cloth. The cab crawled from street to street through every shade of twilight.
At the address, the fog lifted a little and showed a dingy street with a gin shop, a cheap eating house and ragged children. It was hard to believe that this was the home of Jekyll's favourite.

An old woman with silver hair opened the door, and although she had an evil face, her manners were excellent. She said Hyde was out, but when she learned that the visitor was a police inspector, a look of joy crossed her face.
Hyde used only two rooms in the whole house, but they were furnished with luxury and good taste. There was wine in the closet, silver on the table and a fine picture on the wall.

The rooms showed every sign of having been searched in a hurry, with clothes on the floor and drawers standing open. In the ashes of the fire the inspector found a burned cheque-book, and behind the door lay the other half of the stick.
A visit to the bank showed that several thousand pounds lay to the murderer's credit. The inspector told Utterson that he had Hyde in his hand, because a man like Hyde could not live without money.
Finding Hyde was not so easy, because he had few friends and no family that anyone could trace. People who had seen him described him differently, and only one thing was the same in every account.

That afternoon Utterson went to Jekyll's house, and Poole led him across the old garden to a dingy, windowless building. It had once belonged to a famous surgeon, but the doctor now used it for his chemical work.
Utterson crossed the old theatre, where crates and straw now lay on the floor. A flight of stairs led to a red door, and behind it he found Jekyll sitting close to the fire, looking deadly sick.
When Poole had gone, Utterson asked whether Jekyll had heard the news, and the doctor shuddered. Utterson then asked if he was hiding Hyde, and Jekyll swore that he would never set eyes on him again.

Jekyll insisted that Hyde was safe and would never be heard of again. Utterson warned that his name might appear in a trial, and Jekyll replied that he had received a letter and was unsure what to do.

Jekyll said that he no longer cared what became of Hyde and was thinking only of his own good name. Utterson was surprised at such selfishness, but he was relieved by it, and he asked to see the letter.
The note was written in an odd, upright hand and signed Edward Hyde. It said that Dr Jekyll, whom the writer had repaid so badly, need not worry, because Hyde had a sure way to escape.

Jekyll said he had burned the envelope, and that the note had been handed in without a postmark. When Utterson asked whether Hyde had written the disappearance clause, Jekyll nodded and said he had had a terrible lesson.
As he left, Utterson asked Poole about the man who had brought a letter that day. Poole was sure that nothing had come except by post, and that news sent the lawyer away with his fears renewed.
That evening Utterson sat by his fire with his head clerk, Mr Guest, and a bottle of very old wine between them. Guest was a great student of handwriting, and Utterson decided to show him the letter.

Guest said that the murderer's writing was not mad, but odd. A note from Jekyll arrived, and when Guest compared the two, he said the hands were alike but sloped differently, and Utterson's blood ran cold.

A large reward was offered for the capture of Hyde, because the death of Sir Danvers was felt as an injury to the whole city. Even so, Hyde had vanished from the sight of the police as though he had never existed.
Much of Hyde's past was now dug up, and all of it was disreputable. Stories came out of his cruelty, his vile life and his strange friends, but nobody could say where he was.
From the morning of the murder, Hyde was simply blotted out. As time went on, Utterson recovered from his alarm, and he felt that Hyde's disappearance more than paid for the death of Sir Danvers.

Dr Jekyll came out of his seclusion and renewed his old friendships, becoming once more a familiar guest and host. He had always been known for his charity, and now he was equally known for his religion.

Jekyll was busy and spent much time in the open air, and he did a great deal of good. His face seemed to brighten with the knowledge that he was useful, and for more than two months the doctor was at peace.

On the eighth of January, Utterson dined at the doctor's with a small party, and Lanyon was among the guests. The host's eyes travelled from one friend to the other, as they had in the old days when the three were inseparable.
On the twelfth of January, the door was shut against the lawyer, and it was shut again on the fourteenth. Poole said that the doctor was confined to the house and saw no one.
On the fifteenth he tried a third time and was refused again. After two months of seeing his friend almost every day, this return of loneliness weighed heavily on his spirits.
On the fifth night he asked Guest to dine with him, hoping to drive away his gloomy thoughts. The clerk was good company, but even he could not make Utterson forget the shut door.
The next night he walked to Cavendish Square to visit Dr Lanyon, who at least would not refuse to see him. The butler admitted him at once and showed him into the dining room.
The red-faced doctor had grown pale and thin, and his hair had fallen out, and he looked many years older. It was not the sickness that struck Utterson most, however, but the fear in his eyes.

Lanyon said that he had received a shock from which he would never recover, and that it was only a question of weeks. He had once liked life very much, he said, but now he thought he would be glad to leave it.
Utterson mentioned that Jekyll was ill too, and he asked if Lanyon had seen him. Lanyon held up a trembling hand and said that he wished to see or hear no more of Dr Jekyll.

Lanyon said that after his death Utterson might learn the right and wrong of it, but that he could not tell him now. He begged the lawyer either to talk of other things or to go, because he could not bear the subject.
As soon as he reached home, Utterson sat down and wrote to Jekyll. He complained that he had been shut out of the house and asked what had caused the unhappy break with Lanyon.

The next day brought a long, sad and mysterious answer from Jekyll. He wrote that the quarrel with Lanyon could not be mended, that he meant to live in seclusion, and that Utterson must respect his silence.
Utterson was amazed, because only a week ago Jekyll had looked forward to a cheerful and honoured old age. Now friendship and peace of mind were wrecked, and such a change seemed to point to madness.

Inside was a second sealed envelope, marked not to be opened until the death or disappearance of Henry Jekyll. Utterson longed to read it at once, but he felt bound by honour, and he locked it in his safe.
It happened one Sunday that Utterson was out on his usual walk with Mr Enfield. Their way led them once more through the little by-street of shops.
They stopped in front of the shabby door, and Enfield said that at least that story was over. Utterson hoped so, and admitted that he had once met Hyde and had felt the same disgust.
Enfield laughed and said that Utterson must have thought him a fool for not knowing this was a back way to Dr Jekyll's house. He had found it out, he added, partly through Utterson's own fault.
Utterson suggested that they step into the court and look at the windows. He was uneasy about poor Jekyll, he said, and even from outside the presence of a friend might do him good.
The court was cool and a little damp, and it was already full of twilight. High overhead, the sky was still bright with the light of the sunset.
The middle one of the three windows was half open. Sitting beside it, like a sad prisoner taking the air, was Dr Jekyll.

The words were hardly out of his mouth when the smile was wiped from his face. In its place came a look of such terror and despair that the blood of the two men froze.

They left the court without a word and walked in silence through the by-street until they reached a busier road. There they looked at each other, both pale, and Utterson said, “God forgive us,” while Enfield only nodded gravely.
One evening in March, Utterson was sitting by his fire after dinner when he was surprised by a visit from Poole. He asked what had brought him there, and whether the doctor was ill.
Poole said that there was something wrong, and Utterson gave him a chair and a glass of wine. He told the butler to take his time and explain plainly what he wanted.
Poole explained that the doctor had shut himself up in the cabinet again, and that he did not like it. He had been afraid for about a week, he said, and could bear it no longer.
Poole looked terrible, and he never once looked the lawyer in the face. He said hoarsely that he thought there had been foul play, and he asked Utterson to come and see for himself.
Utterson's only answer was to get his hat and greatcoat. He noticed the great relief on the butler's face, and that the wine was still untouched when Poole set it down.
It was a wild, cold night in March, with a pale moon lying on her back as though the wind had tilted her. Thin, torn clouds flew across the sky, and the wind made talking difficult.

The wind seemed to have swept the streets bare, and Utterson had never seen that part of London so deserted. He wished he could see and touch other people, for he felt that some terrible disaster was near.

The square was full of wind and dust, and the thin trees in the garden lashed against the railing. Poole stopped, took off his hat and wiped his forehead with a red handkerchief, though it was not weariness that made him sweat.

Poole knocked in a guarded way, and the door opened on its chain. Inside, all the servants stood huddled around the fire like a flock of sheep, and the cook ran forward crying that Mr Utterson had come.
Utterson said it was very irregular, but Poole told him that the servants were all afraid. Poole took a candle and led him out to the garden, warning him to come gently and not to go in if asked.

Poole led Utterson into the old theatre, among the crates and straw, and knocked on the cabinet door above. He called that Mr Utterson wished to see the doctor, and a complaining voice answered that it could see no one.

Poole whispered to ask if that had been his master's voice, and Utterson said it seemed much changed. Poole answered that after twenty years he could not be deceived, and that his master had been made away with eight days ago.
Utterson said that it was a very wild tale, and he asked why a murderer would stay in the house. That did not seem reasonable, he said, and Poole promised to satisfy him.
Poole explained that for a week the one in the cabinet had begged night and day for a certain medicine. Orders were thrown down on slips of paper, and Poole had been sent to every chemist in London.

Each time Poole brought the drug home, another paper told him it was not pure, and sent him to a new firm. He gave Utterson a crumpled note in which Jekyll begged Messrs Maw to find him some of the old.

Utterson asked why the note was open, and Poole said that the man at Maw's had thrown it back at him angrily. It looked like the doctor's handwriting, said Poole, but he cared more about what he had seen.
Poole said he had walked suddenly into the theatre and seen a figure digging among the crates. It gave a cry like a rat and ran upstairs into the cabinet, and it was wearing a mask.

Utterson thought that Jekyll had a terrible illness that changed his voice and made him wear a mask. Poole turned pale and said it was not his master, who was tall and well built, while this thing was more like a dwarf.

Poole cried that after twenty years he knew exactly where his master's head came to in the cabinet door. He believed that murder had been done, and Utterson decided that it was his duty to break the door down.
Poole fetched the axe from the theatre, and Utterson took the kitchen poker. They agreed that they both thought the masked figure was Hyde, and the lawyer feared that poor Harry had been killed.

Utterson called for Bradshaw, the footman, and told him that he and Poole would force the cabinet door. Bradshaw and the boy were to take sticks and guard the laboratory door, and they were given ten minutes.
When the ten minutes were nearly over, Utterson looked at his watch and followed Poole into the yard. The wind tossed the candle flame about, and the two men sat down in the theatre to wait.

Nearby, the only sound was a footstep moving to and fro along the cabinet floor. Poole whispered that it would walk like that all day and most of the night, with only a short rest when a new sample came.
Poole asked him to listen carefully and say whether it was the doctor's step. The footsteps fell lightly and oddly, with a kind of swing, and they were quite unlike Jekyll's heavy, creaking tread.
Utterson sighed and asked whether there had ever been anything else. Poole said that once he had heard it weeping, like a woman or a lost soul, and that he could have wept himself.
The ten minutes were nearly over, and Poole pulled the axe from under a stack of packing straw. Utterson then called out loudly that he demanded to see Jekyll, by fair means or foul.
A voice from the cabinet cried, “Utterson, for God's sake, have mercy.” The lawyer knew at once that it was not Jekyll's voice but Hyde's, and he ordered Poole to break the door down.
Poole swung the axe over his shoulder, and the blow shook the whole building. A dismal screech of animal terror rang from the cabinet, and four times the axe fell, but the wood was tough.

He was austere with himself and tolerant of others, and he was often the last decent acquaintance a ruined man had left.

The shops stood in a cheerful row with fresh paint, polished brass and bright windows, each one seeming to smile at the passer-by in hope of custom. He asked whether his cousin had ever noticed it before, and remarked that it was connected in his mind with a very odd story.
