He had one more word to add, and he was sure that his friend would take it in good part, which was that this was a private matter and that he begged Utterson to let it sleep. The lawyer looked for a little while into the fire, as though the coals might give him counsel, and then rose to his feet. “I have no doubt you are perfectly right,” he said at last, though he did not truly feel that it was so.

Since they had touched upon the business, said Jekyll, and for the last time he hoped, there was one point he wished the lawyer to understand, and that was that he took a very great interest in poor Hyde. If he himself were taken away, he wanted Utterson to promise that he would bear with the young man and get him his rights, for it would be a weight off his mind. The lawyer replied that he could never pretend to like Hyde, and Jekyll, laying a hand on his arm, said that he asked only for justice, and for help given for his sake.

Utterson heaved an irrepressible sigh, and after a long moment he said that he would promise. He left the house soon afterwards and walked home through the cold, quiet streets, turning the promise over in his mind like a stone he could not set down. He had bound himself to a man whose face he could not forget, and he went to bed uneasy, as one does who has signed a paper without reading it through.

Nearly a year later, in the month of October, London was startled by a crime of singular ferocity, and the shock was made the greater by the high position of the person who had suffered. The details were few, but they were enough to fill the newspapers and the drawing rooms, and for days nobody spoke of anything else. It was one of those crimes that seem to turn the whole city pale and make honest people lock their doors.

A maidservant who lived alone in a house not far from the river had gone upstairs to bed at about eleven o'clock. Though a fog rolled over the city later in the small hours, the early part of the night was cloudless, and the lane which her window overlooked was brilliantly lit by the full moon. It was the sort of night that makes the plainest street look like a stage, and the girl, who was not at all sleepy, did not draw the curtain.

She seemed to be of a romantic turn of mind, and instead of going to bed she sat down on her box beneath the window and fell into a daydream. Never, she said afterwards, with tears streaming down her face, had she felt more at peace with all men, or thought more kindly of the world. The lane lay silent and silver under the moon, and nothing in it gave her the least warning of what she was about to see.

As she sat there, the maid became aware of an aged and beautiful gentleman with white hair, who was drawing near along the lane at a leisurely pace. Advancing to meet him came another gentleman, a very small one, to whom at first she paid little attention, as one pays little to a shadow. The two were soon close together, and when they came within speech, which was just under her eyes, the older man bowed and spoke.

The old gentleman accosted the other with a very pretty manner of politeness, and from the way he pointed it sometimes seemed as if he were only asking the road. The moon shone on his face as he spoke, and the girl watched it with pleasure, for it seemed to breathe such an innocent and old-world kindness of disposition, with something high in it, too, as of well-founded self-content. Nothing in his bearing suggested that he had the faintest notion of danger, and he stood easily on the bright pavement with his hands behind his back.

Presently her eye wandered to the second man, and with a start she recognised him as a certain Mr Hyde, who had once called upon her master and for whom she had at once conceived a dislike. He held in his hand a heavy cane, with which he was playing carelessly, and he answered never a word. He seemed to listen, instead, with an ill-contained impatience, like a man who is forced to stand still when he longs to be moving.

And then, all at once, Hyde broke out in a great flame of anger, stamping with his foot, brandishing the cane and carrying on, as the maid described it, like a madman. The old gentleman took a step backwards, with the air of one who is very much surprised and a little hurt. It was the last courteous gesture of his life, and it seemed only to make the other more furious.

At that Hyde broke out of all bounds and clubbed the old gentleman to the earth, and the next moment, with ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim and raining blows upon him. The sounds of that cruelty rose to the open window and filled the little room. Overcome by the horror of what she heard and saw, the maid fainted and knew no more.

It was two o'clock in the morning when the girl came to herself and called for the police, whose lanterns soon appeared in the lane. The murderer had been gone for a long time, but his victim lay in the middle of the road, so cruelly used that his face was hard to look at. The moon that had been so bright had begun to sink, and the first thin fog was creeping up from the river.

The stick with which the deed had been done was of some rare, tough and heavy wood, and it had snapped in the middle under the stress of that senseless cruelty, leaving one splintered half in the gutter. The other half had plainly been carried away by the murderer, who had not touched his victim's purse or his gold watch. The dead man carried no cards or papers, except one sealed and stamped letter that he had been taking to the post, and that bore the name and address of Mr Utterson.

Next morning, before Utterson had risen from his bed, a police officer arrived at the house with the sealed letter and a brief account of what had happened in the lane. The lawyer said that he would give no opinion until he had seen the body, and he asked the man to wait while he dressed. With the same grave countenance he hurried through his breakfast and drove to the police station, where the dead man had been carried.

When he was shown the body, Utterson said at once that he knew the man, and that, sorry as he was to say it, this was Sir Danvers Carew. The officer exclaimed in horror, and in the next moment his eyes lit up with professional ambition, for he saw that the case would make a great deal of noise. He briefly told the lawyer what the maid had witnessed and then laid before him the broken stick.

Utterson had already quailed at Hyde's name, but when the stick was laid before him he could doubt no longer, for it was a stick that he himself had given to Henry Jekyll years before. He asked whether this Mr Hyde was a person of small stature, and the officer replied that the maid called him particularly small and particularly wicked-looking. Utterson reflected a moment, and then offered to take the officer to the house in his own cab.

By this time it was about nine in the morning, and the first fog of the season hung like a great chocolate-coloured pall over the sky, while the wind charged and routed the vapours without ever dispersing them. As the cab crawled from street to street, Utterson saw a marvellous number of shades of twilight, here dark as the end of evening, there glowing a lurid brown as though some strange fire were burning. His thoughts, meanwhile, were as gloomy as the weather, and when he glanced at the officer beside him he felt something of that terror of the law that may assail even the most honest.

As the cab drew up at the address, the fog lifted a little and showed a dingy street, a gin palace, a low French eating house, a shop for penny numbers and twopenny salads, and many ragged children. Women of many nationalities passed out of the houses, key in hand, to take a morning glass, and then the fog settled down again as brown as umber and shut the lawyer off from his surroundings. This was the home of Henry Jekyll's favourite, the man who was the heir to a fortune of a quarter of a million.

An ivory-faced, silvery-haired old woman opened the door, a woman with an evil face smoothed by hypocrisy, though her manners were excellent. She said that this was indeed Mr Hyde's house, that he was not at home, and that he kept irregular habits, for it was nearly two months since she had seen him until yesterday. When Utterson explained that his companion was Inspector Newcomen of Scotland Yard, a flash of odious joy appeared upon her face, and she cried out to know what Hyde had done.

Of the whole extent of the house, which was otherwise empty but for the old woman, Hyde used only a couple of rooms, but these were furnished with luxury and good taste. A closet was filled with wine, the plate was of silver, the linen elegant, and a good picture hung upon the wall, a gift, Utterson guessed, from Henry Jekyll, who was something of a connoisseur. The carpets were thick and agreeable in colour, and nothing in the rooms matched the man whom Utterson had met in the street.

At this moment, however, the rooms bore every mark of having been recently and hurriedly ransacked, with clothes lying about the floor, their pockets turned inside out, and the drawers standing open. On the hearth lay a pile of grey ashes, as though many papers had been burned, and from these embers the inspector dug out the butt end of a green cheque-book that had resisted the fire. The other half of the stick was found behind the door, and since this settled his suspicions, the officer declared himself delighted.

A visit to the bank, where several thousand pounds were found lying to the murderer's credit, completed the officer's satisfaction. You may depend upon it, he told Utterson, that he already had Hyde in his hand, for the man must have lost his head or he would never have left the stick behind, or above all have burned the cheque-book. Money was life to such a man, and all that remained was to wait for him at the bank and to print the handbills.

This last, however, proved much harder to accomplish, for Hyde had numbered few familiars, his family could be traced nowhere, and he had never been photographed. The few who could describe him differed widely, as common observers will, and only on one point were they all agreed. It was the haunting sense of unexpressed deformity with which the fugitive had impressed everyone who had beheld him.

That same afternoon Utterson went to Jekyll's door, where Poole received him and led him across what had once been a garden to the building at the bottom of it. The block, which was called indifferently the laboratory or the dissecting rooms, had belonged to the heirs of a celebrated surgeon, and Jekyll, whose tastes were chemical rather than anatomical, had changed its purpose. It was the first time that the lawyer had been taken into that part of his friend's quarters, and he eyed the dingy, windowless structure with curiosity.

Utterson crossed the theatre, once crowded with eager students and now gaunt and silent, with crates and packing straw littering the floor. At the further end a flight of stairs mounted to a door covered with red baize, and through this he was received into the doctor's cabinet, a large room fitted round with glass presses. Beside the fire in that dusty, barred room sat Jekyll, looking deadly sick, and he did not rise but held out a cold hand and bade his friend welcome in a changed voice.

As soon as Poole had left them, Utterson asked whether the doctor had heard the news of the murder, and Jekyll shuddered and said that the newsboys had been crying it in the square. The lawyer said that Carew had been his client, and so was Jekyll, and that he wished to know whether his friend had been mad enough to hide the fellow. Jekyll cried out, swearing to God that he would never set eyes on Hyde again, and he bound his honour that he was done with the man in this world.

It was all at an end, said Jekyll, and Hyde did not want his help, for he was safe, quite safe, and would never more be heard of. The lawyer listened gloomily, for he did not like his friend's feverish manner, and he remarked that if the matter ever came to a trial, the doctor's own name might appear. Jekyll replied that he had grounds for certainty which he could share with nobody, but that he had received a letter and wished to leave it in Utterson's hands, because he trusted his judgment so greatly.

Utterson asked whether the doctor feared that the letter might lead to Hyde's capture, and Jekyll said that he did not care what became of the man, for he was quite done with him. He was thinking, he explained, of his own character, which this hateful business had rather exposed. The lawyer ruminated awhile, surprised at his friend's selfishness and yet relieved by it, and then he said that he would see the letter.

The letter was written in an odd, upright hand and signed Edward Hyde, and it said that the writer's benefactor, Dr Jekyll, whom he had so unworthily repaid, need feel no alarm for his safety. He had means of escape, it added, on which he placed a sure dependence. The lawyer liked it well enough, for it put a better colour on the friendship than he had looked for, and he blamed himself for some of his past suspicions.

Utterson asked for the envelope, but Jekyll said that he had burned it before he knew what he was about, and that it had borne no postmark, since the note had been handed in. The lawyer then asked, as a last point, whether it was Hyde who had dictated the terms of the will about the disappearance, and the doctor, seized with a qualm of faintness, shut his mouth tight and nodded. He meant to murder you, Utterson said, and you have had a fine escape, and Jekyll answered that he had had far more than that, for he had had a lesson, and he covered his face with his hands.

On his way out, Utterson asked Poole about the messenger who had handed in a letter that day, but Poole was quite positive that nothing had arrived except by post, and only circulars at that. This news sent the visitor away with his fears renewed, for the letter must have come in through the laboratory door, and it might even have been written in the cabinet. As he walked, the newsboys cried themselves hoarse in the street, and he feared that the good name of another friend might be sucked down into the scandal.

Presently Utterson sat on one side of his own hearthrug, with Mr Guest, his head clerk, on the other, and between them a bottle of a particular old wine that had long dwelt unsunned in the foundations of the house. Outside, the fog still lay upon the drowned city, but the room was gay with firelight, and the lawyer melted by degrees. Mr Guest was a student and critic of handwriting, as well as a man of counsel, and it seemed natural and even obliging to ask for his opinion on the letter.

Guest studied the murderer's autograph with passion and said that it was not the hand of a madman, only an odd one. Just then a servant brought in a note from Dr Jekyll, an invitation to dinner, and the clerk, asking permission, laid the two sheets side by side and compared them with great care. He found them alike in many points and different only in slope, and when he had gone, Utterson locked the letter away and thought with a chill of Jekyll forging for a murderer.

Thousands of pounds were offered as a reward, for the death of Sir Danvers was resented as a public injury, and the handbills appeared on every wall. Yet Mr Hyde had disappeared out of the ken of the police as though he had never existed on this earth. The detectives, who had been so confident of catching him, began to speak of him with a kind of grudging respect.

Much of Hyde's past was unearthed, and all of it was disreputable, for tales came out of his callous cruelty and sudden violence, of his vile way of life and the strange associates who had shared it. Everywhere the story was the same, that of a man surrounded by hatred and followed by whispers of fear. Of his present whereabouts, however, there was not a whisper to be heard, and the trail ran cold at the door of the house in Soho.

From the hour when he left the house in Soho on the morning of the murder, Hyde was simply blotted out, and Utterson began to recover from the heat of his alarm. In his own way of thinking, the death of Sir Danvers was more than paid for by the disappearance of the man who had caused it. Now that the evil influence had been withdrawn, he hoped that a new life might begin for his old friend Dr Jekyll.

Jekyll came out of his seclusion, renewed his friendships and became once more a familiar guest and entertainer in the houses of his friends. He had always been known for his charities, but now he was no less distinguished for his religion, and he spoke of such matters with a plain and humble sincerity that touched all who heard him. It seemed as though a heavy door had been opened in the house of his mind, and the light of the common day had been let in.

He was busy, he was much in the open air, and he did good in many quiet ways, so that his face seemed to open and brighten as if with an inward consciousness of service. Those who had known him well said that he had grown ten years younger, though in a different way from what youth had ever meant to him. For more than two months, Jekyll was at peace, and it seemed that the dark chapter of his life had ended.

On the eighth of January, Utterson dined at the doctor's with a small party, and Lanyon was among the guests. The host's eye travelled from one friend to the other as it had in the old days, when the three had been inseparable, and the talk was easy and the wine was good. For a little while the lawyer allowed himself to believe that every old trouble had been forgotten, though it was the last time that the three of them ever sat together.

But on the twelfth, and again on the fourteenth, the door of the doctor's house was shut against the lawyer, and Poole said, with an uneasy face, that Dr Jekyll was confined to the house and saw no one. Utterson could scarcely believe it, for the friend who had welcomed him so warmly only days before now would not even come down to the hall. He went away puzzled, and a little hurt, and he could not help thinking that something was wrong.

On the fifteenth he tried again and was again refused, and the sound of the door closing before his face seemed to him louder than any door had a right to be. For two months he had been used to seeing his friend almost daily, and this sudden return of solitude lay heavily upon his spirits. A man who lives alone and asks little of the world will sometimes miss a single face more than a crowd.

On the fifth night he invited Guest to dine with him, hoping that the company of a sensible man would drive away the gloomy thoughts that crowded about him. The clerk was a pleasant guest and talked well on many subjects, but even he could not make Utterson forget the closed door in the square. When the cloth was cleared, the lawyer had made up his mind to seek advice from another quarter.

On the sixth night he put on his coat and went to Dr Lanyon's house in Cavendish Square, hoping that there, at least, he would find the welcome he had been refused elsewhere. He was not denied admittance, and the butler took him at once into the dining room, where the doctor sat alone with his wine. Utterson had expected to find his old friend as hale and loud as ever, and he was not prepared for what he saw.

The rosy man of a few weeks ago had grown pale, his flesh had fallen away, he was visibly balder and older, and yet it was not these signs of swift decay that struck the lawyer. It was a look in the eye and a change in the manner that seemed to speak of some deep-seated terror of the mind. It was hard to believe that a man who feared death so little in his profession should now look so much like one who is already condemned.

“I have had a shock,” said Lanyon in a thin voice, “and I shall never recover from it, for it is only a question of weeks. Life has been pleasant,” he went on, “and I used to like it very much, but I sometimes think that if we knew everything, we should be more glad to get away.” Utterson noticed that, for all his courage, the doctor could not keep his hands from shaking.

Utterson said that Jekyll also was ill, and he asked whether Lanyon had seen him lately, and at this the face of the other changed. Lanyon held up a trembling hand and said, in a loud, unsteady voice, that he wished to see or hear no more of Dr Jekyll. He was quite done with that person, he declared, and he begged the lawyer to spare him any mention of one whom he regarded as dead.

“Tut, tut, can nothing be done,” said Utterson, “for we are three very old friends, Lanyon, and we shall not live long enough to make others.” “Nothing can be done,” answered Lanyon, who told the lawyer to ask Jekyll himself, and when Utterson said that Jekyll would not see him, he replied that he was not surprised. There was something in his tone that made it plain that he knew much more than he would say.

“Some day, Utterson, after I am dead, you may perhaps come to learn the right and wrong of this,” said the doctor, “but I cannot tell you now. In the meantime, if you can talk with me of other things, then for God's sake stay, but if you cannot keep clear of this accursed topic, then in God's name go, for I cannot bear it.” The lawyer, who could not bring himself to leave a dying friend, stayed, and the two of them spoke of nothing at all until midnight.

As soon as he reached home, Utterson sat down and wrote to Jekyll, complaining gently of his exclusion from the house in the square and asking what had caused the unhappy break with Lanyon. He was not a man who wrote many letters, and he spent a long time over this one, trying to find words that would be kind and yet would ask a plain question. When it was done, he sealed it with a heavy heart and put it out for the morning post.

The next day brought a long answer, often very pathetically worded and sometimes darkly mysterious in its drift. The quarrel with Lanyon was incurable, Jekyll wrote, and from now on he meant to live in extreme seclusion, so that his friend must not doubt his friendship if his door was often shut. He had brought on himself a punishment and a danger that he could not name, and the only thing that Utterson could do to lighten it was to respect his silence.

Utterson was amazed, for the dark influence of Hyde had been withdrawn, the doctor had returned to his old tasks and friendships, and a week before the prospect had smiled with every promise of a cheerful and honoured age. Now, in a moment, friendship, peace of mind and the whole course of his life were wrecked. So great and unprepared a change pointed to madness, but in view of Lanyon's manner and words, the lawyer felt that there must lie a deeper reason.

A week afterwards Dr Lanyon took to his bed, and in something less than a fortnight he was dead. On the night after the funeral, at which he had been sadly affected, Utterson locked the door of his business room and drew out an envelope addressed in the hand and sealed with the seal of his dead friend. It was marked for Utterson alone and, in case of his death, to be destroyed unread, and the lawyer dreaded to see the contents, but he condemned his fear as a disloyalty and broke the seal.

Within there was another enclosure, likewise sealed, and marked on the cover as not to be opened until the death or disappearance of Dr Henry Jekyll. Utterson could not trust his eyes, for here again, as in the mad will, were the idea of a disappearance and the name of Jekyll set side by side. A great curiosity came upon him to break the seal and dive to the bottom of these mysteries, but honour and faith to his dead friend were stringent obligations, and the packet slept in his safe.

It chanced on a Sunday that Utterson was out on his customary walk with Enfield, and as the two cousins talked of small things, their way led them once more into the little by-street of shops. The winter had passed, the shutters were closed for the day of rest, and the narrow street lay quiet in the thin sunshine. Neither of them had planned it, yet each of them felt that something was drawing them towards the one place they had agreed never to mention.

As they came opposite the shabby door, both stopped to look at it, and Enfield remarked that at least that story was at an end and they would never see any more of Mr Hyde. Utterson said that he hoped so, and he told his cousin that he had once seen the man himself, and had shared his feeling of repulsion. “It was impossible to do the one without the other,” returned Enfield, and the two of them stood a moment looking at the blistered panels in thoughtful silence.

Enfield added with a rueful laugh that Utterson must have thought him an ass, for he had not known until lately that this was a back way into the house of Dr Jekyll. It was partly Utterson's own fault that he had found it out, even when he did. The lawyer answered that he was glad to hear it, since it saved him the trouble of explaining much that he would rather have left unsaid.

So he had found it out, the lawyer said, and in that case they might as well step into the court and take a look at the windows. To tell the truth, he was uneasy about poor Jekyll, and even from outside he felt that the presence of a friend might do the man good. Enfield, who had always disliked the place, followed him in silence, though with a reluctant and dragging step upon the cold flagstones.

The court was very cool and a little damp, and it was full of a premature twilight, though the sky high overhead was still bright with the last of the sunset. The three windows on the first floor looked down on it like blind eyes, and the whole place had a stillness that seemed to hold its breath. Even the sound of the city had faded to a murmur, as if it did not care to come so near.

The middle one of the three windows was half open, and sitting close beside it, taking the air with an infinite sadness of manner like some disconsolate prisoner, Utterson saw Dr Jekyll. He called out the doctor's name in glad surprise and said that he trusted his friend was better. The face at the window seemed a good deal thinner than he remembered, and the eyes were hollow.

“I am very low, Utterson,” replied the doctor drearily, “very low, and it will not last long, thank God.” The lawyer said that he stayed too much indoors, and, having introduced his cousin, he told Jekyll to get his hat and take a quick turn with them. The doctor leaned his head against the frame and seemed to listen with great attention.

“You are very good,” sighed Jekyll, “and I should like it of all things, but no, it is quite impossible, and I dare not.” He was glad to see them, he said, and would have asked them up, but the place was really not fit for visitors. The lawyer, good-naturedly, said that the best they could do was to stay down in the court and speak from where they were, and the doctor, with a smile, said that was just what he had been about to propose.

But the words were hardly uttered before the smile was struck out of his face and succeeded by an expression of such abject terror and despair as froze the very blood of the two gentlemen below. They saw it only for a glimpse, for the window was instantly thrust down, and the court was left empty and silent. Whatever had passed behind that glass had been quicker than a thought, and it had left no mark except upon their minds.

That glimpse had been enough, and without a word they turned and left the court. In silence they crossed the by-street, and it was not until they reached a neighbouring thoroughfare, where even on a Sunday there were still some stirrings of life, that Utterson turned at last and looked at his companion. They were both pale, and there was an answering horror in their eyes, and Utterson said, “God forgive us, God forgive us,” while Enfield only nodded his head very seriously and walked on in silence.

One evening, as Utterson sat by his fireside after dinner, he was surprised by a visit from Poole, who had never before come to the house in the course of twenty years. The lawyer asked what had brought him there, and then, looking at the butler more closely, he asked what was the matter with him, and whether the doctor was ill. It was clear from the first glance that the man was labouring under some great strain.

Poole said that there was something wrong, and Utterson, who knew that the butler was not a man to be easily alarmed, made him sit down and poured him a glass of wine. He told him to take his time and to say plainly what he wanted, and he waited with growing unease for the answer. The fire crackled in the grate, and the clock on the mantelpiece seemed suddenly very loud in the silent room.

“You know the doctor's ways, sir, and how he shuts himself up,” said Poole, “but he is shut up again in the cabinet, and I wish I may die if I like it.” When Utterson asked him to be explicit, the man disregarded the question and answered doggedly that he had been afraid for about a week. “And I can bear it no more, Mr Utterson,” he added, and the lawyer saw that his hands were trembling as he said it.

The man's appearance amply bore out his words, for his manner had altered for the worse, and except for the moment when he first announced his terror, he had not once looked the lawyer in the face. Even now he sat with the glass of wine untasted on his knee and his eyes fixed on a corner of the floor. “I think there has been foul play,” he said hoarsely, “but I daren't say more, sir, and I ask you to come along with me and see for yourself.”

Utterson's only answer was to rise and fetch his hat and greatcoat, and as he did so he observed with wonder the greatness of the relief that appeared upon the butler's face. He noticed, too, that the glass of wine remained untasted when Poole set it down to follow him. It seemed to him that nothing short of real terror could make a hungry, chilled man leave good wine untouched.

It was a wild, cold, seasonable night of March, with a pale moon lying on her back as though the wind had tilted her, and a flying wrack of the thinnest and most transparent cloud. The wind made talking difficult and whipped the blood into the face, and the two men walked with their heads bent, saying nothing. Everything about that night seemed to Utterson to have been arranged for some terrible purpose.

The wind seemed to have swept the streets unusually bare of passers-by, and Utterson thought that he had never seen that part of London so deserted. He could have wished it otherwise, for never in his life had he felt so sharp a longing to see and touch his fellow-creatures. Struggle as he might against the feeling, there was borne in upon his mind a crushing expectation of calamity.

The square was full of wind and dust, and the thin trees were lashing themselves along the railing, when Poole, who had kept a pace ahead all the way, stopped in the middle of the pavement. In spite of the biting cold he took off his hat and mopped his brow with a red handkerchief, but it was the sweat of anguish that he wiped away. His face was white and his voice harsh and broken as he said, “Well, sir, here we are, and God grant there be nothing wrong.”

Poole knocked in a very guarded manner, the door was opened on the chain, and a voice from within asked whether it was he. In the hall, which was brightly lighted, with the fire built high, the whole of the servants, men and women, stood huddled together about the hearth like a flock of sheep. At the sight of Mr Utterson the housemaid broke into hysterical whimpering, and the cook, crying out that it was he, ran forward as if she meant to take him in her arms.

Utterson said peevishly that all this was very irregular and unseemly, but Poole replied that they were all afraid, and the maid, who began to weep loudly, was told sharply to hold her tongue. Then the butler took a candle and led the way to the back garden, begging the lawyer to come as gently as he could, for he wished him to hear, but not to be heard. “And see here, sir,” he whispered, “if by any chance he was to ask you in, don't go.”

Poole led the lawyer into the old theatre, among the crates and packing straw, to the foot of the stair that climbed to the cabinet, and there he set down the candle. He struck the door and called out in a loud voice that Mr Utterson was asking to see the doctor, and a voice answered from within, complaining and thin, telling them that it could see no one. “Thank you, sir,” said Poole, with something very like triumph in his voice, and he turned a white face to the lawyer in the candlelight.

“Was that my master's voice,” whispered Poole, and the lawyer, very pale but giving look for look, replied that it seemed much changed. “Have I been twenty years in this house to be deceived about his voice,” said Poole, “no, sir, he was made away with eight days ago, when we heard him cry out upon God.” “And who is in there instead of him, and why it stays, is a thing that cries to Heaven.”

Utterson, biting his finger, said that this was a wild tale, for if the doctor had indeed been killed, it was hard to see why the murderer should stay. Such a theory would not hold water, he added, and it did not commend itself to reason. Poole answered that the lawyer was a hard man to satisfy, but that he would do it yet.

All this last week, said Poole, whoever or whatever lived in that cabinet had been crying night and day for some kind of medicine and could not get it to his liking. It was the master's way to write his orders on paper and throw them down the stair, and all week they had had nothing but papers, a closed door, and meals left outside to be smuggled in. Every day, and sometimes thrice in one day, there had been orders and complaints, and Poole had been sent flying to every wholesale chemist in town.

Every time he brought the stuff back, said Poole, there would be another paper telling him to return it as not pure, and another order to a different firm, and the drug was wanted bitter bad, whatever it was for. He drew from his pocket a crumpled note, and Utterson, bending to the candle, read that Dr Jekyll presented his compliments to Messrs Maw and found their latest sample impure and quite useless. He begged them to search with care for any of the old quality, and at the end, with a splutter of the pen, he wrote, “For God's sake, find me some of the old.”

“This is a strange note,” said Utterson, and he asked how Poole came to have it open, and the butler replied that the man at Maw's had been angry and had thrown it back at him. The lawyer said that it was unquestionably the doctor's hand, and Poole answered, rather sulkily, that it looked like it, but he added in a different voice that handwriting mattered nothing, since he had seen him. Utterson, startled, repeated the words and asked him to explain, and Poole drew a long breath and began his tale.

Poole said that he had come suddenly into the theatre from the garden, and that there, at the far end, someone had been digging among the crates for the drug. The creature looked up when he entered, gave a kind of cry and whipped upstairs into the cabinet, and though Poole had seen it for only a minute, the hair had stood upon his head like quills. Why, he asked, if that was his master, had it a mask upon its face, and why had it cried out like a rat and run from him.

Utterson said that he began to see daylight, for his friend was plainly seized by one of those maladies that torture and disfigure, which explained the changed voice, the mask and the hunt for a drug. It was sad enough, but plain and natural, and it delivered them from all exorbitant alarms. “Sir,” said the butler, turning to a sort of mottled pallor, “that thing was not my master, and there is the truth, for my master is a tall, fine build of a man, and this was more of a dwarf.”

Poole cried that he had known his master for twenty years and knew just where his head came to in the cabinet door, where he had seen him every morning of his life. That thing in the mask was never Dr Jekyll, God knew what it was, and it was the belief of his heart that there had been murder done. The lawyer replied gravely that it was now his duty to make certain, and that he would break in that door, and Poole, with a cry of approval, said that he would help him.

Poole said that there was an axe in the theatre, and the lawyer could take the kitchen poker, which Utterson weighed in his hand before remarking that they were placing themselves in some danger. Both of them thought more than they had said, so they made a clean breast, and Poole confessed that the masked creature had the same size and quick, light manner as Mr Hyde. “I believe that poor Harry is killed,” said Utterson, “and that his murderer is still lurking in his victim's room.”

Utterson called for the footman, Bradshaw, who came very white and nervous, and told him to pull himself together, for it was now their intention to make an end of the suspense. He and Poole would force their way into the cabinet, he said, and if all was well, his shoulders were broad enough to bear the blame. Bradshaw and the boy were to go round the corner with a pair of good sticks and stand at the laboratory door, and they were given ten minutes to reach their posts.

Utterson looked at his watch and, when the time was nearly up, took the poker under his arm and led the way into the yard, where the scud had banked over the moon and it was now quite dark. The wind, which only broke in puffs and draughts into that deep well of building, tossed the candle to and fro about their steps until they came into the shelter of the theatre. There they sat down silently to wait, while London hummed solemnly all round them.

Nearer at hand the stillness was broken only by the sound of a footfall moving to and fro along the floor of the cabinet. “So it will walk all day, sir,” whispered Poole, “and the better part of the night, and only when a new sample comes from the chemist is there a bit of a break.” He added that it was an ill conscience that was such an enemy to rest, and that there was blood foully shed in every step of it.

“Hark again, a little closer,” whispered Poole, “put your heart in your ears, Mr Utterson, and tell me, is that the doctor's foot.” The steps fell lightly and oddly, with a certain swing, for all they went so slowly, and they were different indeed from the heavy creaking tread of Henry Jekyll. Utterson, listening with all his attention, was obliged to admit that the butler was right.

Utterson sighed and asked whether there had never been anything else, and Poole nodded and said, “Once, I heard it weeping.” When the lawyer, conscious of a sudden chill of horror, asked what he meant, the butler said that it had wept like a woman or a lost soul. “I came away with that upon my heart,” he said, “that I could have wept too.”

But now the ten minutes drew to an end, and Poole disinterred the axe from beneath a stack of packing straw and set the candle on the nearest table to light them to the attack. They drew near with bated breath to where that patient foot was still going up and down, and Utterson cried in a loud voice, “Jekyll, I demand to see you.” He paused a moment, but there came no reply, and he went on, “I give you fair warning, and I must and shall see you, if not by fair means, then by foul.”

“Utterson,” said the voice, “for God's sake, have mercy,” and the lawyer, who had half hoped to hear the doctor's familiar tones, knew at once that this thin, broken cry belonged to someone else. “Ah, that is not Jekyll's voice,” he cried in sudden certainty, “it is the voice of Hyde.” Then, turning to the butler, he shouted that they must have the door down at once, whatever it might cost them.

Poole swung the axe over his shoulder, and the blow shook the building and made the red baize door leap against its lock and hinges. A dismal screech, as of mere animal terror, rang from the cabinet, and up went the axe again, and again the panels crashed and the frame bounded. Four times the blow fell, but the wood was tough and the fittings were of excellent workmanship.

It was not until the fifth blow that the lock burst and the wreck of the door fell inwards on the carpet, and the besiegers, appalled by their own riot and the stillness after it, peered in. There lay the cabinet before their eyes, with a good fire glowing on the hearth, the kettle singing its thin strain, a drawer or two open and the papers neatly laid out. Near the fire stood the things laid ready for tea, and but for the glazed presses full of chemicals, it was the quietest and most commonplace room in London that night.

Right in the middle of the floor lay the body of a man, and when they drew near on tiptoe and turned him on his back, they beheld the face of Edward Hyde. He was dressed in clothes far too large for him, clothes of the doctor's bigness, and though the muscles of his face still moved with a semblance of life, life was quite gone. By the crushed phial in his hand and the strong smell of kernels in the air, Utterson knew that he was looking at the body of a self-destroyer.

Utterson said sternly that they had come too late, whether to save or to punish, and that it only remained to find the body of Poole's master. Most of the building was taken up by the theatre and the cabinet, but there were also a few dark closets and a spacious cellar, and all of these they now examined. Each closet needed only a glance, for all were empty and had plainly stood long unopened, and the cellar, filled with crazy lumber, was sealed by a perfect mat of cobweb that fell when they opened its door.

Nowhere in all that building was there any trace of Henry Jekyll, either dead or alive, and the butler stamped upon the flags of the corridor, listening for a hollow sound. “He must be buried here,” he said gloomily, and the sound of his boot rang along the stone like a muffled bell. Utterson answered that he might equally have fled, and he turned to examine the door that opened on the by-street.

The door was locked, and lying near it on the flags they found the key, already stained with rust and snapped in two, as though a man had trodden on it with all his weight. “This does not look like use,” observed the lawyer, and Poole answered that it was broken, and the fractures were rusty too. The two men looked at each other with a scare, and Utterson admitted that this was beyond him, and proposed that they go back to the cabinet.

They mounted the stair in silence and, with an occasional awestruck glance at the dead body, examined the cabinet more thoroughly. At one table there were traces of chemical work, and various measured heaps of a white salt lay on glass saucers, as though in preparation for an experiment which the unhappy man had been prevented from completing. “That is the same drug that I was always bringing him,” said Poole, and even as he spoke the kettle boiled over with a startling noise.

This brought them to the fireside, where the easy-chair was drawn cosily up and the tea things stood ready to the sitter's elbow, the very sugar already in the cup. Several books stood on a shelf, and one lay open beside the tea things, and Utterson was amazed to find that it was a copy of a pious work for which Jekyll had often expressed great esteem. It was annotated, in his own hand, with such startling blasphemies that Utterson could scarcely believe what he saw.

Next, in the course of their review, the searchers came to the tall mirror, and into its depths they looked with an involuntary horror. It was so turned as to show them nothing but the rosy glow on the ceiling, the fire sparkling along the glazed presses, and their own pale and fearful faces stooping to look in. “This glass has seen some strange things, sir,” whispered Poole, and the lawyer replied in the same tone that none of them could be stranger than the glass itself.

On the business table, among the neat array of papers, a large envelope lay uppermost, and it bore in the doctor's hand the name of Mr Utterson. The lawyer unsealed it, and several enclosures fell to the floor, the first of them a will, drawn up in the same eccentric terms as the one he had returned six months earlier. In place of the name of Edward Hyde, however, he read, with indescribable amazement, the name of Gabriel John Utterson.

He looked at Poole, and then at the paper, and last of all at the dead malefactor stretched upon the carpet, and said that his head went round. For days Hyde had been in possession, he had no cause to like Utterson, and he must have raged to see himself displaced, yet he had not destroyed the document. Then the lawyer caught up the next paper, a brief note in the doctor's hand with a date at the top, and cried that Jekyll must have been alive and in this room that very day.

Poole asked why he did not read it, and the lawyer replied solemnly that he feared what it might say. “My dear Utterson,” it began, “when this falls into your hands, I shall have disappeared, though how I cannot foresee, and the end is sure and must be early.” He was to read first the narrative that Lanyon had been told to place in his hands, and then, if he cared to hear more, the confession of his unworthy and unhappy friend, Henry Jekyll.

There was a third enclosure, asked Utterson, and Poole handed over a considerable packet sealed in several places, which the lawyer put in his pocket. He said that he would say nothing of the papers, since if the doctor had fled or was dead they might at least save his credit. It was now ten o'clock, and he must go home to read these documents in quiet, but he would be back before midnight, when they would send for the police.

Utterson went home, took the packet from his safe and sat down by the fire to read what his dead friend had written. On the ninth of January, wrote Lanyon, a registered envelope had come by the evening delivery, addressed in the hand of his old schoolfellow Henry Jekyll. He was surprised, for the two were not in the habit of writing, and he had dined with Jekyll the night before and could imagine nothing that justified the formality.

Dear Lanyon, the letter began, you are one of my oldest friends, and though we have differed on scientific questions, I cannot remember on my side any break in our affection. There was never a day when, if you had told me that your life or honour depended upon me, I would not have sacrificed my left hand to help you. Now my life, my honour and my reason are all at your mercy, Lanyon, and if you fail me tonight, I am lost.

“You might suppose,” the letter went on, “that I am about to ask something dishonourable, but judge for yourself.” Lanyon was to put aside every other engagement, even if he were summoned to the bedside of an emperor, and to drive straight to the house, where Poole would be waiting with a locksmith. The door of the cabinet was then to be forced, and Lanyon was to go in quite alone, with nobody to witness what he did.

Within the cabinet, Lanyon was to open the glazed press marked with the letter E, breaking the lock if it were shut, and to draw out the fourth drawer from the top, with all its contents just as they stood. In his distress, Jekyll wrote, he had a morbid fear of misdirecting him, but even if he were in error, Lanyon would know the right drawer by its contents, which were some powders, a phial and a paper book. This drawer he begged his friend to carry back to Cavendish Square exactly as it stood.

The second part of the service, wrote Jekyll, was that at midnight Lanyon must be alone in his consulting room and admit with his own hand a man who would come in Jekyll's name. Lanyon was to place in the man's hands the drawer he had brought, and within five minutes, if he wished an explanation, he would understand that these fantastic arrangements were of capital importance. By neglecting any one of them he might charge his conscience with Jekyll's death or the shipwreck of his reason.

“Think of me at this hour,” Jekyll wrote, “in a blackness of distress, yet certain that, if you serve me punctually, my troubles will roll away like a story that is told.” A postscript added that the post office might fail him and the letter might arrive only the next morning, in which case Lanyon should still expect the messenger at midnight. If that night passed without event, the postscript ended, then Lanyon would know that he had seen the last of Henry Jekyll.

Upon reading this letter, Lanyon wrote, he made sure that his colleague was insane, but until that was proved beyond the possibility of doubt, he felt bound to do as he was asked. The less he understood of the farrago, the less he was able to judge its importance, and an appeal so worded could not be set aside without grave responsibility. He rose from the table, got into a cab and drove straight to Jekyll's house.

The butler was awaiting his arrival, having received by the same post a registered letter of instruction, and he had already sent for a locksmith and a carpenter. The tradesmen arrived while they were still speaking, and the whole party moved to old Dr Denman's surgical theatre, from which Jekyll's private cabinet is most conveniently entered. The door was very strong and the lock excellent, and the carpenter said that he would have to do much damage if force were used, while the locksmith was near despair.

But the locksmith proved a handy fellow, and after two hours of work the door stood open. The press marked E was unlocked, and Lanyon took out the drawer, filled it up with straw to keep the contents from moving, tied it in a sheet and returned with it to Cavendish Square. He felt, as he drove through the lamplit streets with the drawer on his knees, that he was playing a part in a play whose plot he did not know.

Here he proceeded to examine the contents, and found that the powders, though neatly made up, were not wrapped with the nicety of a dispensing chemist, so that they were plainly of Jekyll's private manufacture. One wrapper, when opened, held what seemed to be a simple crystalline salt of a white colour. The phial, which was perhaps half full of a blood-red liquor, was highly pungent to the smell and seemed to Lanyon to contain phosphorus and some volatile ether.

The book was an ordinary version book and contained little but a series of dates, which covered a period of many years, though the entries had ceased abruptly nearly a year before. Here and there a single word was added to a date, so that double appeared perhaps six times in several hundred entries, and once, long before, came the words total failure, with several marks of exclamation. All of this whetted Lanyon's curiosity, but it told him little that was definite.

Here were a phial of salt and the record of experiments that had led, like too many of Jekyll's investigations, to nothing of practical use. Lanyon wondered how such things could touch the honour or life of his flighty colleague, and the more he reflected, the more he was convinced that he was dealing with a case of brain disease. Though he sent his servants to bed, he loaded an old revolver, that he might be found in some posture of self-defence.

Hardly had the bells of London rung out midnight when a very gentle tap sounded on the door, and Lanyon went himself and found a small man crouching against the pillars of the portico. When asked whether he came from Dr Jekyll, the man said yes by a constrained gesture, and when invited to enter, he did so only after a searching glance back into the dark square. A policeman stood not far off, advancing with his lantern open, and at the sight the visitor seemed to start and hurry.

These particulars struck Lanyon disagreeably, and as he followed his visitor into the bright light of the consulting room, he kept his hand ready upon his weapon. Here at last he saw him clearly, and he was struck by the shocking expression of his face, by his mixture of strength and weakness, and above all by the odd disturbance caused by his nearness. It resembled a rising chill, and was accompanied by a marked sinking of the pulse.

This person, who had from the first moment of his entrance excited in Lanyon what he could only call a disgustful curiosity, was dressed in a fashion that would have made any ordinary man laughable. His clothes, though of rich and sober material, were enormously too large for him, the trousers rolled up to keep them from the ground and the collar sprawling wide upon his shoulders. Strange to relate, the ludicrous costume was far from moving Lanyon to laughter, for there was something in the wearer that forbade it.

“Have you got it,” cried the stranger, “have you got it,” and so lively was his impatience that he laid his hand upon Lanyon's arm and tried to shake him. Lanyon put him back, conscious at his touch of an icy pang along his blood, and reminded him coldly that they had not yet been introduced. He then sat down in his customary seat, with as fair an imitation of his ordinary manner to a patient as the hour, the nature of his thoughts and his horror of the visitor would allow.

“I beg your pardon, Dr Lanyon,” he answered civilly, “for my impatience has shown its heels to my politeness, and I come at the instance of your colleague, Dr Jekyll, on business of some moment.” He paused and put his hand to his throat, and Lanyon could see, in spite of his collected manner, that he was wrestling against the approaches of hysteria. “I understood that there was a drawer,” he managed to say at last, in a voice that was almost a whisper.

Lanyon took pity on his visitor's suspense, and perhaps on his own growing curiosity, and pointed to the drawer where it lay on the floor behind a table, still covered with the sheet. The man sprang to it and then paused, laying his hand upon his heart, and Lanyon could hear his teeth grate with the convulsive action of his jaws. His face was so ghastly to see that the doctor grew alarmed for both his life and his reason, and begged him to compose himself.

He turned a dreadful smile upon Lanyon and, as if with the decision of despair, plucked away the sheet, and at the sight of the contents he uttered one loud sob of such immense relief that Lanyon sat petrified. Then, in a voice already fairly well under control, he asked for a graduated glass, measured out a few drops of the red tincture and added one of the powders. The mixture began to brighten in colour as the crystals melted, to boil audibly and to throw off small fumes, and suddenly it turned dark purple, and faded slowly to a watery green.

The stranger said that Lanyon might be wise and let him leave without further parley, or he might stay, and then his sight would be blasted by a prodigy to stagger the unbelief of Satan. “I have gone too far in the way of inexplicable services,” said Lanyon, “to pause before I see the end.” The man drank at one gulp, his face turned dark and his features seemed to melt, and when Lanyon had leaped back against the wall, there stood before him, pale and shaken, Henry Jekyll.

“What he told me in the next hour I cannot bring my mind to set on paper,” wrote Lanyon. “I saw what I saw and I heard what I heard, and my soul sickened at it, and my life is shaken to its roots.” He felt that his days were numbered, he added, and he would die incredulous, and the creature who had crept into his house was, on Jekyll's own confession, Hyde, hunted everywhere as the murderer of Carew.

Utterson sat for a long time in silence, and then, with a hand that was none too steady, he broke the seals of the packet and began to read. “I was born to a large fortune,” wrote Jekyll, “endowed with excellent gifts and fond of the respect of the wise and good, and so with every guarantee of an honourable future.” The worst of his faults, he confessed, was a certain impatient gaiety of disposition, which he found hard to reconcile with his wish to carry his head high before the public.

Hence it came about, he wrote, that he concealed his pleasures, and that when he began to take stock of his position in the world, he stood already committed to a profound duplicity of life. Many a man would have boasted of such irregularities, but he, with his high views, hid them with an almost morbid sense of shame. Though he was a deep double-dealer, he was no hypocrite, for he was no more himself when he plunged into disgrace than when he laboured by daylight to relieve suffering.

His scientific studies, he wrote, led wholly towards the mystic and the transcendental, and they shed a strong light upon the perpetual war among the parts of his nature. From both sides of his mind, the moral and the intellectual, he drew steadily nearer to the truth that was to wreck him, that man is not truly one, but truly two. He said that he put it as two only because the state of his own knowledge went no further, and that others would follow and outstrip him on the same lines.

From an early date, he wrote, he had dwelt with pleasure, as on a beloved daydream, on the thought of separating these two elements. If each could be housed in a separate identity, life would be relieved of all that was unbearable, for the unjust might go his way, freed from the remorse of his upright twin. And the just might walk steadfastly on his upward path, doing the good things in which he found pleasure, for it was the curse of mankind, he thought, that these incongruous natures were bound together.

In the course of his laboratory researches, Jekyll wrote, he found that certain agents had the power to shake and pluck back the fleshly covering of the spirit, as a wind might toss the curtain of a pavilion. He did not publish his discovery, for he knew that an excess of dose, or a moment of ill luck, might shatter the frail tabernacle of identity that the drug sought to change. Yet the temptation of so singular and profound a discovery at last overcame his alarms.

The tincture had long been prepared, he wrote, and he purchased a large quantity of a particular salt from a firm of wholesale chemists, knowing it to be the last ingredient required. Late one accursed night he compounded the elements, watched them boil and smoke together in the glass, and when the bubbling had died down, with a strong glow of courage, he drank off the potion. It was a step he could not have taken in the light of day.

There followed, he wrote, the most racking pangs, a grinding in the bones, a deadly nausea and a horror of the spirit that cannot be exceeded at the hour of birth or death. Then the agonies began swiftly to subside, and he came to himself as if out of a great sickness, conscious of something indescribably new and, from its very novelty, incredibly sweet. He felt younger, lighter and happier in body, and within him was a heady recklessness and an unknown freedom of the soul that was not an innocent one.

He knew himself at the first breath of this new life to be more wicked, tenfold more wicked, sold a slave to his original evil, and the thought in that moment braced and delighted him like wine. Stealing through the sleeping house, a stranger in his own home, he came to his bedroom and saw for the first time the appearance of Edward Hyde, a man much smaller, slighter and younger than Henry Jekyll. As good had shone upon Jekyll's face, so evil was written broadly upon the face of Hyde.

When he looked upon that ugly idol in the glass, Jekyll wrote, he was conscious of no repugnance, but rather of a leap of welcome, for this too was himself, and it seemed natural and human. He saw that no one could come near Hyde without a visible shrinking of the flesh, because all other human beings are a mixture of good and evil, and Edward Hyde alone in the ranks of mankind was pure evil. Then he hurried back to the cabinet, prepared and drank the cup a second time, and came to himself once more with the stature and the face of Henry Jekyll.

That night, Jekyll wrote, he had come to the fatal crossroads, for had he approached his discovery in a nobler spirit, he might have come forth from those agonies an angel instead of a fiend. The drug had no power to choose, being neither diabolical nor divine, and it did no more than shake the doors of the prison of his nature, so that whatever stood within ran forth. At that time his virtue slumbered, while his evil, kept awake by ambition, was swift to seize the moment, and the thing that was set free was Edward Hyde.

Although he now had two characters as well as two appearances, one was wholly evil and the other was still the old Henry Jekyll, that incongruous compound whose improvement he had learned to despair of. His pleasures were undignified, to say the least, and as he was well known, highly considered and growing old, the incoherence of his life was daily more unwelcome. It was on this side that the new power tempted him, since he had only to drink the cup to shed the body of the famous professor and put on that of Edward Hyde like a thick cloak.

He smiled at the idea, which seemed humorous to him at the time, and made his preparations with the most studious care. He took and furnished that house in Soho to which Hyde was later tracked by the police, and engaged as housekeeper a creature whom he knew to be silent and unscrupulous. At home he told his servants that a Mr Hyde was to have full liberty in the house, and to avoid accidents he called there himself, until he was a familiar sight in his second character.

He next drew up the will to which Utterson had so much objected, so that if anything befell him as Dr Jekyll, he could enter upon the life of Edward Hyde without loss of money. Others had hired villains to do their crimes while they sat in safety, but he was the first who could strip off respectability like a schoolboy and spring headlong into the sea of liberty. If danger came, Hyde would pass away like the stain of breath upon a mirror, and in his place a man who could afford to laugh at suspicion would sit quietly at home, Henry Jekyll.

The pleasures that he made haste to seek in his disguise were, as he had said, undignified, but in the hands of Edward Hyde they soon began to turn towards the monstrous. This familiar that he had called out of his own soul was a being inherently malign, whose every thought was centred on himself, and who drank pleasure with bestial greed from any pain that another suffered. Jekyll stood at times aghast before the acts of Hyde, but his conscience slept, for it was Hyde, after all, and Hyde alone, who was guilty.

Of those infamies he had no wish to speak, but he mentioned one accident, an act of cruelty to a child that roused a passer-by, whom he later recognised as Utterson's kinsman. To calm the child's relatives, Hyde had been forced to pay them with a cheque in the name of Henry Jekyll, and to prevent such danger in future, Jekyll opened an account in Hyde's name. By sloping his own handwriting backward he gave his double a signature, and he thought that he sat beyond the reach of fate.

Some two months before the murder of Sir Danvers, Jekyll wrote, he had returned from one of his adventures late and woken next day in bed with somewhat odd sensations. In vain he looked about at the decent furniture and tall proportions of his room in the square, for something kept insisting that he lay in the little room in Soho where he slept in the body of Edward Hyde. Then his eyes fell upon his hand, which should have been large, firm and comely, but which was lean, corded, dusky and thickly shaded with hair, and it was the hand of Edward Hyde.

He stared at the hand for some minutes in stupid wonder before terror woke in his breast like the crash of cymbals. Bounding from the bed, he rushed to the mirror and saw that he had gone to bed Henry Jekyll and awakened Edward Hyde, while all his drugs lay in the cabinet across the court. Then he remembered, with sweet relief, that the servants knew his second self, so he dressed, hurried past the staring Bradshaw, and ten minutes later sat down as Dr Jekyll to a pretence of breakfast.

His appetite was small, for this strange event seemed like the writing on the wall at Babylon, spelling out the letters of his judgment, and it showed that he was losing hold of his better self. Between the two he now felt that he must choose, because they shared their memory but little else, and Hyde was as indifferent to Jekyll as a mountain bandit to his cave. As with most tempted sinners, he chose the better part and was found too weak to keep it, for he gave up neither the house in Soho nor the clothes of Hyde.

For two months, however, Jekyll was true to his decision, living a life of such severity as he had never before attained and enjoying the rewards of an approving conscience. But time began to wear away the freshness of his alarm, the praises of conscience became a matter of course, and he was tortured by throes and longings, as of Hyde struggling after freedom. At last, in an hour of moral weakness, he once again mixed and swallowed the draught, and his devil, who had been long caged, came out roaring.

Even as he took the draught, Jekyll wrote, he was conscious of a more furious readiness for evil, and it must have been this that stirred the tempest of impatience with which he heard his victim's civilities. He declared before God that no man morally sane could have committed that crime upon so pitiful a provocation. He had struck, he said, in no more reasonable a spirit than that in which a sick child may break a plaything.

When weariness began to follow his frenzy, Jekyll wrote, Hyde was suddenly struck through the heart by a cold thrill of terror, and he saw that he had forfeited his life. He fled from the scene, glorying and trembling, ran to the house in Soho and burned his papers, and then wandered the lamplit streets in a divided ecstasy. He gloated over his crime while he listened behind him for the steps of the avenger, and he sang as he mixed the draught and pledged the dead man as he drank.

The pangs of transformation had not done tearing Hyde before Henry Jekyll, with streaming tears of gratitude and remorse, had fallen on his knees and lifted his clasped hands to God. The veil of self-indulgence was rent from head to foot, and he saw his life as a whole, from the days of childhood to the horrors of that evening. He could have screamed aloud, and he sought with tears and prayers to smother the crowd of hideous images with which his memory swarmed.

Soon afterwards he locked the door in the by-street and ground the key under his heel, and next day came news that the murder had been witnessed, and that the victim was a man of high standing. It had been not only a crime but a tragic folly, and he was glad to have his better impulses buttressed by the terrors of the scaffold, for Jekyll was now his city of refuge. He resolved to redeem the past by his future conduct, and for a time the days passed quietly, almost happily.

It was a fine, clear January day, wet underfoot where the frost had melted but cloudless overhead, and the Regent's Park was full of winter chirrupings and sweet with spring odours. Jekyll sat in the sun on a bench, comparing his active goodwill with the lazy cruelty of his neighbours, and in the very moment of that vainglorious thought a qualm came over him, a horrid nausea and a deadly shuddering. When it passed he looked down and saw that his clothes hung formlessly on his shrunken limbs and that the hand upon his knee was corded and hairy, and he knew that he was once more Edward Hyde.

A moment before he had been safe in all men's respect, wealthy and beloved, and now he was the common quarry of mankind, hunted, houseless, a known murderer and thrall to the gallows. Hyde reasoned with himself, took a room at a hotel in Portland Street and wrote two letters, one to Lanyon and one to Poole, and to make sure that they were sent he had them registered. Then he sat all day over the fire in the private room, gnawing his nails and dining alone with his fears, until night came and he rode in the corner of a closed cab about the streets of the city.

When he came to himself in Lanyon's house, Jekyll wrote, it was no longer the fear of the gallows but the horror of being Hyde that racked him, and he received Lanyon's condemnation partly in a dream. He slept profoundly that night, and woke shaken and weakened but refreshed, glad to be at home and close to his drugs. Yet after breakfast, as he crossed the courtyard, the old shudder seized him again, and it took a double dose to recall him to himself, and six hours later the pangs returned and the drug had to be taken again.

From that day forth, he wrote, it seemed only by an effort like gymnastics, and only with the help of the drug, that he could wear the countenance of Jekyll. At all hours he would be taken with the warning shudder, and if he slept, or even dozed for a moment in his chair, it was always as Hyde that he woke. Under the strain of this impending doom and of his sleeplessness, he became a creature eaten up by fever, weak in body and mind, and occupied by one thought alone, the horror of his other self.

The hatred between them, Jekyll wrote, was equal on each side, for he saw in Hyde a horror knit to him closer than a wife, while Hyde loathed Jekyll and played ape-like tricks upon him. Then came the last calamity, for his supply of the salt, which had never been renewed since the first experiment, began to run low, and when he sent for a fresh supply and mixed the draught, it was without effect. London had been ransacked in vain, and he was now persuaded that his first supply had been impure and that this unknown impurity had given the draught its power.

“About a week has passed,” wrote Jekyll, “and I am finishing this statement under the influence of the last of the old powders.” “This is the last time, short of a miracle, that Henry Jekyll can think his own thoughts or see his own face, now so sadly altered, in the glass.” He could not say whether Hyde would die upon the scaffold or find the courage to end it, and, laying down the pen, he wrote, “I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end.”
